Non-deterministic LLM work before interrupt changes the draft
Generate in a separate node and save the draft in state
The approve node interrupts with the stored draft
Send in a later node

steps.overview: This step teaches you to make agent behaviour visible and measurable with LangSmith. You will turn on tracing, read traces to debug prompts, tool calls, latency and tokens, then build datasets and run experiments that score prompt changes. The LangSmith course and real agent work both expect you to prove an improvement with numbers, not by feel.
objectives: Enable LangSmith tracing for any LangChain or LangGraph app using LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY.
Read a trace tree to find the exact prompt, tool call, latency and token cost of each step.
Create a dataset of examples and write code and LLM-as-judge evaluators.
Run and compare experiments with evaluate() to show a score change caused by a prompt edit.
Version prompts and debug a local agent in LangSmith Studio with langgraph dev and langgraph.json.

concepts.explanation: Setting LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY makes LangChain and LangGraph send every run to LangSmith automatically, with no code change. LANGSMITH_PROJECT picks the project the traces land in. For plain Python functions or non-LangChain SDK calls, add the @traceable decorator from langsmith.

A trace is one end-to-end request, shown as a tree of runs. Each run has a type such as chain, llm, tool or retriever, plus inputs, outputs, start and end time, and errors. For a create_agent graph you see the model node, each tool call and its arguments, and the loop back to the model.

Each LLM run records latency and token usage (prompt and completion tokens) and, where the model is priced, estimated cost. The trace view rolls these up to the parent, so you can spot the slow step or the call that blew up the context. Use this to justify middleware like SummarizationMiddleware or a cheaper model.

A dataset is a named collection of examples. Each example has inputs (what the target receives) and optional reference outputs (the expected answer). You can create examples in code with Client.create_examples, upload a CSV, or add runs from production traces to a dataset.

An evaluator is a function that scores one run. In the Python SDK it can take inputs, outputs and reference_outputs and return a bool, a number or a dict with a key and score. Use code evaluators for exact checks (format, keyword, tool used) and LLM-as-judge for open-ended quality.

openevals provides create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model=..., feedback_key=...) which returns an evaluator that asks a judge model to grade the output against the reference. Prebuilt prompts like CORRECTNESS_PROMPT save time, but you should spot-check judge scores against your own judgement.

evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]) runs the target on every example, applies every evaluator and saves the results as one experiment. Use experiment_prefix to name it, for example prompt-v1. Two experiments on the same dataset can be opened side by side in the comparison view to see per-example wins, losses and aggregate scores.

LangSmith stores prompts with a commit history; you push new versions and pull a specific version or tag in code, so experiments map to exact prompt versions. LangSmith Studio connects to your agent running locally via the LangGraph CLI (langgraph dev) using a langgraph.json config. In Studio you can run the graph, inspect state at each node, step through interrupts and edit inputs.

keyFacts: Minimum tracing setup: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY=<key>; add LANGSMITH_PROJECT to choose a project, otherwise traces go to the default project.
LangChain and LangGraph code is traced automatically once the env vars are set; use @traceable for your own functions.
An example = inputs + optional reference outputs; a dataset is a set of examples; an experiment = one run of a target over a dataset with evaluators.
evaluate(target, data=..., evaluators=[...], experiment_prefix=...) is the core API; the target takes the example inputs dict and returns an outputs dict.
Evaluator arguments by name: inputs, outputs, reference_outputs; return a bool, a number, or a dict with key and score.
openevals: create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model=..., feedback_key="correctness") for an LLM-as-judge evaluator.
Decision rule: compare two prompts on the same dataset, with the same evaluators and the same model; change only one thing per experiment.
LangSmith Studio needs langgraph.json (dependencies, graphs, env) and the local server started with langgraph dev.
Use the comparison view to read per-example regressions, not just the average score.

example.caption: Build a 20-example dataset and compare two system prompts with an LLM-as-judge correctness evaluator.
example.code:
# env: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true, LANGSMITH_API_KEY=..., plus model provider keys
from langsmith import Client, evaluate
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from openevals.llm import create_llm_as_judge
from openevals.prompts import CORRECTNESS_PROMPT

PAIRS = [("How do I reset my password?", "Use Settings > Security > Reset.")]  # extend to 20 pairs
V1 = "You are a support bot."
V2 = "You are a support bot. Answer in 2 sentences using only product facts. Say 'I don't know' if unsure."

client = Client()
ds = client.create_dataset("support-faq-20")
client.create_examples(dataset_id=ds.id, examples=[
    {"inputs": {"question": q}, "outputs": {"answer": a}} for q, a in PAIRS])

model = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", temperature=0)

def make_target(system_prompt):
    def target(inputs: dict) -> dict:
        msg = model.invoke([{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
                            {"role": "user", "content": inputs["question"]}])
        return {"answer": msg.content}
    return target

judge = create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model="openai:o3-mini", feedback_key="correctness")
def correctness(inputs, outputs, reference_outputs):
    return judge(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs, reference_outputs=reference_outputs)

for name, sp in [("prompt-v1", V1), ("prompt-v2", V2)]:
    evaluate(make_target(sp), data="support-faq-20", evaluators=[correctness],
             experiment_prefix=name, max_concurrency=4)

pitfalls: Setting only the API key and forgetting LANGSMITH_TRACING=true, so nothing appears in the UI.
Changing the prompt and the model (or temperature) in the same experiment, so you cannot say which change moved the score.
Trusting an LLM judge blindly; always read a few low and high scored examples to confirm the judge agrees with you.
A target that returns a string instead of a dict, or uses keys that the evaluator does not read, breaking scoring.
Quoting the average only; a better mean can hide new failures on specific examples that the comparison view would show.
Putting secrets in langgraph.json; reference an .env file through the env field instead.

files.code:
# gst-agent-evals (Step 6: LangSmith trace and evaluate)

Goal: show a score that improved because of a prompt change.

## Files
- `agent.py` - GST agent built with `create_agent`, plus PROMPT_V1 and PROMPT_V2.
- `setup_langsmith.py` - creates the 20-example dataset `gst-totals-v1` and pushes both prompts to the Prompt Hub as `gst-agent-system`.
- `run_experiment.py` - runs `evaluate()` once per prompt and prints the average scores.
- `langgraph.json` - lets `langgraph dev` load the agent into LangSmith Studio.

## Steps
1. Copy `.env.example` to `.env`. Set `LANGSMITH_TRACING=true`, `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`.
2. `python setup_langsmith.py` - check the dataset under Datasets & Experiments.
3. `python run_experiment.py` - two experiments appear: `gst-prompt-v1-...` and `gst-prompt-v2-...`.
4. In the dataset page, select both experiments and click Compare.

## Reading a trace
Open the project `gst-agent` in LangSmith. Each agent call is one trace made of runs:
- the model run shows the system prompt, user message and any tool call it asked for;
- the tool run `calculate_gst` shows inputs and the returned total;
- each run shows latency, and model runs show token counts (input and output).
With v1 the model often answers without calling the tool. With v2 you see a tool run in every trace.

## Evaluators
- `exact_total` (code): the reference total appears in the answer.
- `used_tool` (code): the agent called `calculate_gst`.
- `correctness` (LLM-as-judge via openevals `CORRECTNESS_PROMPT`).

## Checkpoint
The script prints a table such as `v1 used_tool 0.40 -> v2 used_tool 1.00`. Your numbers will differ. Show the Compare view to prove the change.

## Studio
Run `langgraph dev`. Studio opens with graph `gst_agent` (prompt v2). Send a question, step through nodes and inspect state.

"""GST helper agent. Used by the experiments and by LangSmith Studio."""
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.tools import tool

load_dotenv()  # reads LANGSMITH_TRACING, LANGSMITH_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY

MODEL = "openai:gpt-4.1-mini"

# Prompt v1: baseline. Vague, so the model may skip the tool and guess.
PROMPT_V1 = "You are a friendly shop assistant. Help the customer with their question."

# Prompt v2: the change we want to measure.
PROMPT_V2 = (
    "You are a GST calculator for Indian shops. "
    "Always call the calculate_gst tool to get the total. "
    "Never do the arithmetic yourself. "
    "Reply with one line: 'Total: Rs <number>' using the tool result exactly."
)

PROMPTS = {"v1": PROMPT_V1, "v2": PROMPT_V2}


@tool
def calculate_gst(amount: float, rate_percent: float) -> float:
    """Return the total price including GST, rounded to 2 decimals."""
    return round(amount * (1 + rate_percent / 100), 2)


def build_agent(system_prompt: str):
    # create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph (model node + tools node)
    return create_agent(MODEL, tools=[calculate_gst], system_prompt=system_prompt)


# Exported for langgraph.json so `langgraph dev` can show it in Studio.
# No checkpointer here: the Agent Server handles persistence itself.
graph = build_agent(PROMPT_V2)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Quick smoke test; with tracing on, this creates one trace in LangSmith
    out = graph.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Rs 1000 with 18% GST?"}]})
    print(out["messages"][-1].content)

"""Create the 20-example dataset and version both prompts in LangSmith."""
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langsmith import Client

from agent import PROMPTS

load_dotenv()

DATASET = "gst-totals-v1"
PROMPT_NAME = "gst-agent-system"

# 20 (amount, GST rate %) pairs. Rates 5, 18 and 40 are used for variety.
PAIRS = [(1000, 18), (250, 5), (1499, 18), (89.5, 5), (12000, 40),
         (560, 18), (75, 5), (3200, 18), (999, 40), (45, 5),
         (18000, 18), (640, 5), (2750, 40), (130, 18), (5600, 5),
         (810, 18), (2299, 40), (15, 5), (7425, 18), (360, 40)]

# Different phrasings so the dataset is not too easy
TEMPLATES = [
    "What is the total for an item costing Rs {a} with {r}% GST?",
    "Price is {a} rupees before tax. GST is {r}%. How much does the customer pay?",
    "Add {r} percent GST to Rs {a}. Final amount?",
    "Bill: Rs {a} + {r}% GST. Total please.",
]


def main() -> None:
    client = Client()  # uses LANGSMITH_API_KEY

    if client.has_dataset(dataset_name=DATASET):
        print(f"Dataset {DATASET} already exists, skipping.")
    else:
        ds = client.create_dataset(dataset_name=DATASET, description="Total price incl. GST")
        examples = [
            {
                "inputs": {"question": TEMPLATES[i % 4].format(a=a, r=r)},
                "outputs": {"total": round(a * (1 + r / 100), 2)},  # reference answer
            }
            for i, (a, r) in enumerate(PAIRS)
        ]
        client.create_examples(dataset_id=ds.id, examples=examples)
        print(f"Created {DATASET} with {len(examples)} examples.")

    # Prompt versioning: each push becomes a new commit of the same prompt
    for version, text in PROMPTS.items():
        prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([("system", text)])
        try:
            url = client.push_prompt(PROMPT_NAME, object=prompt, description=f"system prompt {version}")
            print(f"Pushed {version}: {url}")
        except Exception as err:  # pushing an unchanged prompt is rejected
            print(f"Skip {version}: {err}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Run one experiment per prompt on the same dataset and compare scores."""
import re

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langsmith import evaluate
from openevals.llm import create_llm_as_judge
from openevals.prompts import CORRECTNESS_PROMPT

from agent import PROMPTS, build_agent
from setup_langsmith import DATASET

load_dotenv()

# LLM-as-judge: grades the answer against the reference output
judge = create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model="openai:gpt-4.1", feedback_key="correctness")


def make_target(system_prompt: str):
    agent = build_agent(system_prompt)

    def target(inputs: dict) -> dict:
        result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": inputs["question"]}]})
        calls = sum(len(getattr(m, "tool_calls", None) or []) for m in result["messages"])
        return {"answer": result["messages"][-1].content, "tool_calls": calls}

    return target


def exact_total(outputs: dict, reference_outputs: dict) -> bool:
    # Code evaluator: does the reference total appear in the answer?
    nums = [float(n.replace(",", "").rstrip(".")) for n in re.findall(r"\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", outputs["answer"])]
    return any(abs(n - reference_outputs["total"]) < 0.01 for n in nums)


def used_tool(outputs: dict) -> bool:
    # Code evaluator: did the agent call calculate_gst?
    return outputs["tool_calls"] > 0


def correctness(inputs: dict, outputs: dict, reference_outputs: dict):
    return judge(inputs=inputs["question"], outputs=outputs["answer"],
                 reference_outputs=f"Total: Rs {reference_outputs['total']}")


scores = {}
for version, prompt in PROMPTS.items():
    results = evaluate(
        make_target(prompt),
        data=DATASET,
        evaluators=[exact_total, used_tool, correctness],
        experiment_prefix=f"gst-prompt-{version}",  # experiment name in the UI
        metadata={"prompt_version": version},
        max_concurrency=4,
    )
    df = results.to_pandas()
    scores[version] = {k: df[f"feedback.{k}"].astype(float).mean()
                       for k in ("exact_total", "used_tool", "correctness")}

# Checkpoint: show the score change caused by the prompt change
for key in scores["v1"]:
    print(f"{key:12} v1 {scores['v1'][key]:.2f} -> v2 {scores['v2'][key]:.2f}")

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the LangSmith course in LangChain Academy: observability (tracing, reading runs) and evaluation (datasets, evaluators, experiments, comparison). There is no proctored exam, so the real test is the notebook work, the checkpoint and follow-up interviews. These ask you to debug a missing or confusing trace, design a fair prompt A/B experiment, and defend an evaluation result with per-example evidence.

compare.difference: A trace is the whole tree for one top-level request. A run is a single step inside it, such as an LLM call, a tool call or a chain.
compare.chooseA: Pick trace when the question is about end-to-end latency or the full story of one user request.
compare.chooseB: Pick run when you need to find which single step was slow, failed or used the most tokens.

compare.difference: A code evaluator is deterministic, cheap and repeatable, but it only checks things you can write rules for. An LLM judge can grade open-ended quality, but it costs money, can drift and must be spot-checked against human judgement.
compare.chooseA: Pick a code evaluator for exact match, valid JSON, required keywords, the correct tool being called or length limits.
compare.chooseB: Pick an LLM judge for correctness or helpfulness of free-text answers, where many wordings can be right.

compare.a: Average score in the experiment list
compare.difference: The average tells you which version is better overall. The comparison view shows which specific examples improved or regressed between experiments.
compare.chooseA: Use the average for a quick ranking of experiments.
compare.chooseB: Use the comparison view before you ship, to catch new failures hidden behind a better mean.

compare.difference: LangChain and LangGraph objects are traced automatically once LANGSMITH_TRACING=true is set. Plain Python functions and raw SDK calls only appear if you decorate them with @traceable.
compare.chooseA: Use @traceable when your own helper or retrieval function is missing from the trace tree.
compare.chooseB: Rely on automatic tracing when the code is already create_agent, a LangGraph graph or LangChain runnables.

compare.difference: Studio is an interactive local IDE for a running graph: you can step through it, inspect state, edit and re-run. The tracing UI is for after-the-fact inspection of runs that were logged to a project.
compare.chooseA: Pick Studio to debug graph flow, state or interrupts on your laptop while you iterate.
compare.chooseB: Pick the tracing UI to review production or experiment runs, latency, tokens and errors.

cues.cue: API key set but no traces in the UI
cues.pick: Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true (and check LANGSMITH_PROJECT)
cues.why: The key alone only authenticates; tracing must be switched on, and traces may be landing in a different project.

cues.cue: Which prompt is better, fairly
cues.pick: Two experiments on the same dataset with the same evaluators and model; only the prompt changes
cues.why: Controlling every other variable is the only way to say the prompt caused the score change.

cues.cue: Scores are all empty or zero after evaluate()
cues.pick: Check that the target returns a dict and that its keys match what the evaluator reads
cues.why: Evaluators read outputs and reference_outputs by key, so a plain string or a mismatched key breaks scoring.

cues.cue: Grade free-text answers against a reference answer
cues.pick: create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT
cues.why: Exact match fails on paraphrases, while a judge compares meaning.

cues.cue: Agent feels slow; find the cause
cues.pick: Open the trace and sort the child runs by latency
cues.why: Run-level latency shows whether the model call, a tool or a retry loop is the bottleneck.

cues.cue: Costs jumped after a change
cues.pick: Token metadata on LLM runs in the trace
cues.why: Per-run prompt and completion tokens show which call grew, for example a longer system prompt or extra tool loops.

cues.cue: Set up Studio for a local agent
cues.pick: langgraph.json with dependencies, graphs and env pointing to .env, then run langgraph dev
cues.why: Studio connects to the local Agent Server that the CLI starts from this config.

cues.cue: Average went up; is it safe to ship?
cues.pick: Check regressions in the comparison view first
cues.why: A higher mean can hide new failures on important examples.

scenario.situation: Your team has a support agent built with create_agent. A teammate rewrote the system prompt and also switched to a cheaper model, then reported that a 20-example experiment's correctness score rose from 0.70 to 0.80. The judge is an openevals LLM-as-judge. Your manager asks whether the new prompt should be shipped. What should you do?
reasoning: Two variables changed at once, prompt and model, so the 0.10 gain cannot be credited to the prompt.
Rerun the experiment with the old model and the new prompt, using the same dataset and the same evaluator, so that only one thing differs.
Open the comparison view and list the examples that went from pass to fail, not just the overall mean.
Read a few high-scored and low-scored examples to confirm the LLM judge agrees with human judgement.
Remember that 20 examples is small: a 2-example swing looks like a 10-point change, so treat small gaps with caution.
scenario.answer: Do not ship yet. Rerun with only the prompt changed, then confirm the gain in the comparison view and with a spot-check of the judge before you claim the prompt improved the score.

memoryAids: Tracing needs 'T-K-P': Tracing=true, Key, Project (optional, but always check it).
Experiment = D-T-E: Dataset + Target + Evaluators. Change ONE knob per run.
Evaluator signature 'I-O-R': inputs, outputs, reference_outputs. Return a bool, a number, or a dict with key and score.
cheatSheet: No traces? Check LANGSMITH_TRACING=true first, then the API key, then which project you are viewing.
LangChain and LangGraph code is traced automatically; decorate your own Python functions with @traceable.
A trace is one request tree; runs are its steps. Find bottlenecks at run level.
Use token metadata on LLM runs to explain cost changes.
The target receives the inputs dict and must return an outputs dict whose keys match what the evaluators read.
Use code evaluators for anything rule-checkable; use an LLM judge only for open-ended quality.
Spot-check the LLM judge on both high-scored and low-scored examples before trusting it.
Use experiment_prefix to give experiments readable names, e.g. prompt-v1 and prompt-v2.
Fair comparison means the same dataset, evaluators, model and temperature; change only the prompt.
Read the comparison view for per-example regressions before you claim an improvement.
Studio needs langgraph.json and langgraph dev. Keep secrets in .env, referenced through the env field.
Version prompts so every experiment maps to an exact prompt version you can roll back to.
selfCheck: I can turn on tracing in a fresh environment and see a run in the project I chose.
I can open a trace and say which run was slowest and which used the most tokens.
I can build a 20-example dataset and write a target that returns a correctly keyed outputs dict.
I can write one code evaluator and one LLM-as-judge evaluator and run both with evaluate().
I can run two experiments that differ only by prompt and show an improved score, with per-example evidence from the comparison view.
I can start Studio with langgraph dev from a langgraph.json that keeps secrets in .env.

objective.question: You set up a fresh Python project with a LangChain v1 agent and want every run to appear in LangSmith. What is the minimum configuration?
options: Set LANGSMITH_PROJECT only; the API key is read from the LangChain config file
Set LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT and call langsmith.init() at startup
Wrap every agent call in @traceable and pass the API key as an argument
Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY=<key>
objective.explanation: The minimum tracing setup is LANGSMITH_TRACING=true plus LANGSMITH_API_KEY. LANGSMITH_PROJECT is optional and only selects the project. LangChain code needs no @traceable, and there is no required init() call.

objective.question: A teammate enabled tracing correctly, but all traces from the 'support-bot' app are mixed with other apps in the 'default' project. What is the most likely cause?
options: LANGSMITH_PROJECT was not set, so traces went to the default project
The agent was built with create_agent instead of StateGraph
The API key belongs to a different workspace
LANGSMITH_TRACING was set to 1 instead of true
objective.explanation: If LANGSMITH_PROJECT is not set, traces go to the default project. Setting LANGSMITH_PROJECT=support-bot routes them to their own project. A wrong workspace key would send the traces to that other workspace, not to this one's default project.

objective.question: Your create_agent calls are traced, but a plain Python function clean_query() that runs before the agent does not appear in the trace tree. How do you fix this?
options: Set LANGSMITH_TRACING_V2=true
Pass callbacks=[LangSmithTracer()] into create_agent
Decorate clean_query() with @traceable from langsmith
Convert clean_query() into a LangGraph node
objective.explanation: LangChain and LangGraph code is traced automatically. Your own functions need the @traceable decorator to appear as runs. The other options are unnecessary, or they are older or invented APIs.

objective.question: Which custom evaluator signature will LangSmith's evaluate() correctly fill with the example's expected answer?
options: def exact(prompt, completion, label):
def exact(input, output, ground_truth):
def exact(inputs, outputs, reference_outputs):
def exact(run, example, expected):
objective.explanation: Evaluator arguments are matched by name: inputs, outputs and reference_outputs. Names like expected, label or ground_truth are not recognised, so they will not receive the reference answer.

objective.question: You call evaluate(target, data="faq-20", evaluators=[correct]). Each example's inputs look like {"question": "..."}. Which target is correct?
options: def target(example) -> None: example.outputs = agent_answer(example.inputs)
def target(inputs: dict) -> str: print(agent_answer(inputs["question"]))
def target(inputs: dict) -> dict: return {"answer": agent_answer(inputs["question"])}
def target(question: str) -> str: return agent_answer(question)
objective.explanation: The target takes the example's inputs dict and returns an outputs dict, which evaluators then receive as outputs. Returning a bare string, None or a print does not give evaluators a structured outputs dict.

objective.question: In LangSmith terminology, what is an experiment?
options: A single trace of one user request
One run of a target over a dataset, scored by evaluators
A set of examples with inputs and reference outputs
A saved version of a prompt in the prompt hub
objective.explanation: An experiment is one run of a target over a dataset, with evaluators scoring the results. A set of examples is a dataset, a single request is a trace, and a saved prompt is a prompt version.

objective.question: You want to know whether prompt B is better than prompt A. Which experiment design is valid?
options: Prompt A and prompt B on the same dataset, with the same evaluators and the same model
Prompt B with an extra LLM-as-judge evaluator that prompt A did not use
Prompt A on last week's dataset, prompt B on an updated dataset with 5 new examples
Prompt A with gpt-4o-mini, prompt B with a larger model, same dataset
objective.explanation: To credit a score change to the prompt, change only one thing per experiment. Keep the dataset, evaluators and model fixed. Every other option changes a second variable, so the result is confounded.

objective.question: Experiment B's average correctness is 0.80, the same as experiment A. The product owner asks if B is safe to ship. What should you do next?
options: Open the comparison view and check per-example regressions and improvements
Delete the low-scoring examples and re-run
Add more evaluators until the averages differ
Ship it, because equal averages mean equal quality
objective.explanation: The same average can hide some examples that got worse and others that got better. The comparison view shows per-example regressions, so you can judge whether the failures B introduces are acceptable. Deleting examples or adding evaluators to force a difference is not valid evaluation.

objective.question: Which snippet creates an LLM-as-judge correctness evaluator with openevals, logging the score under the name 'correctness'?
options: LLMJudge(criteria="correctness", llm=ChatOpenAI())
create_llm_as_judge(CORRECTNESS_PROMPT).score("correctness")
load_evaluator("correctness", model="openai:o3-mini")
create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model="openai:o3-mini", feedback_key="correctness")
objective.explanation: openevals provides create_llm_as_judge, which takes prompt, model and feedback_key arguments. CORRECTNESS_PROMPT is the built-in correctness prompt. The other options are older APIs or invented ones.

objective.question: You want to debug your LangGraph agent step by step in LangSmith Studio on your laptop. What do you need?
options: A Dockerfile and the command langsmith studio --local
Only LANGSMITH_TRACING=true; Studio opens automatically from a trace
A langgraph.json with dependencies, graphs and env, then start the local server with langgraph dev
Deploy to the Agent Server first; Studio cannot connect to local code
objective.explanation: Studio connects to a locally running agent served by the LangGraph CLI. You start it with langgraph dev, using a langgraph.json that declares dependencies, graphs and env. No cloud deployment or special Docker command is required.

objective.question: A trace for one agent request takes 9 s. The root run shows 9 s. Two child LLM runs show 1.5 s each, and a child tool run 'search_orders' shows 5.8 s. What is the best first optimisation target?
options: Switch to a faster model
Turn off tracing, since it adds most of the overhead
Investigate the search_orders tool, which dominates the latency
Shorten the system prompt to cut LLM latency
objective.explanation: A trace is a tree of runs, and each child run shows its own latency. Here the tool run takes about 5.8 of the 9 seconds, so it is the bottleneck. Prompt or model changes would save little, and tracing does not add seconds of latency.

objective.question: Your dataset examples have inputs but no reference outputs. Which evaluator can still work as designed?
options: An LLM-as-judge that grades conciseness or helpfulness using only inputs and outputs
CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, which requires a reference answer
None; evaluate() refuses datasets without reference outputs
An exact-match evaluator comparing outputs to reference_outputs
objective.explanation: Reference outputs are optional in an example. Evaluators that only need inputs and outputs, such as a reference-free LLM judge for conciseness, still work. Exact match and a reference-based correctness judge need reference_outputs.

objective.question: You run `langgraph dev` and the CLI fails with an error saying it cannot find the graph 'agent'. Your file src/agent.py defines `graph = create_agent(...)`. What is the most likely fix to this langgraph.json?
options: Change the value to "./src/agent.py:graph" so it points at the compiled graph variable
Remove "env" because Studio cannot read .env files
Replace "dependencies" with a requirements.txt path only
Rename the key "graphs" to "agents"
objective.explanation: Each entry under "graphs" must use the form path:variable so the CLI knows which object is the compiled graph. The key name "graphs" is correct, and "env" pointing to .env is valid. The dependencies value ["."] is also valid.

objective.question: Your team stores the support prompt in LangSmith and edits it often. You want next week's experiment rerun to use exactly the same prompt text as today's run. What should your evaluation code do?
options: Copy the prompt into a Python string and delete it from LangSmith
Set LANGSMITH_PROJECT to the prompt name so the version is locked
Pull the prompt pinned to a specific commit hash (or a tag you never move), and record it in experiment metadata
Pull the prompt by name only, which always returns the latest commit
objective.explanation: Pinning to a commit hash makes the experiment reproducible, and logging it in metadata links scores to the prompt version. Pulling by name only returns whatever the latest commit is. LANGSMITH_PROJECT controls where traces go, not prompt versions.

objective.question: You run evaluate() with this evaluator. Under which feedback key will the scores appear in the experiment results?
options: score
correctness
exact_match
check_answer
objective.explanation: When an evaluator returns a dict with a "key" field, LangSmith uses that value as the feedback name. The function name is used only when no key is given. "score" is the value field, and "correctness" is unrelated.

objective.question: Your LLM-as-judge scores change from run to run on the same 20 examples, so a small gap between prompt A and prompt B is hard to trust. Which evaluate() change directly reduces this noise?
options: Pass num_repetitions=3 so each example runs several times and scores can be averaged
Add a different experiment_prefix to each run
Turn off LANGSMITH_TRACING during the experiment
Set max_concurrency=1 so examples run one by one
objective.explanation: num_repetitions runs each example several times, so you can see variance and average out random judge and model noise. max_concurrency only controls parallelism. experiment_prefix only names the experiment, and turning off tracing would stop the experiment from being recorded properly.

objective.question: Product wants to filter production traces by customer tier ('free' or 'pro') in the LangSmith UI. The agent is a create_agent graph. What is the simplest correct approach?

code.code:
result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": q}]},
    config={ ??? },
)

options: {"recursion_limit": "pro"}
{"thread_id": "pro"}
{"metadata": {"tier": "pro"}, "tags": ["support-bot"]}
{"configurable": {"tier": "pro"}}
objective.explanation: Run metadata and tags passed in the config are attached to the trace, and you can filter by them in LangSmith. configurable is for runtime parameters such as thread_id, not trace filtering. recursion_limit controls the step limit. thread_id at the top level is the wrong place and is not meant for filtering.

objective.question: An agent runs inside a short-lived serverless function. Tracing is enabled, but some traces never appear in LangSmith, especially for fast requests. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: LangSmith drops traces shorter than one second; add a sleep to the agent
Serverless functions cannot reach LangSmith; tracing only works on servers
Traces are sent in the background and the process exits before they are sent; flush pending traces (for example with wait_for_all_tracers()) before returning
The API key expires after each call; create a new key per request
objective.explanation: The SDK sends traces asynchronously, so a function that exits immediately can lose unsent runs. Flushing before the handler returns fixes this. API keys do not expire per call, and LangSmith does not drop short traces.

objective.question: What does this code produce in LangSmith?

code.code:
from langsmith import evaluate

for name, target in [("prompt-a", run_a), ("prompt-b", run_b)]:
    evaluate(
        target,
        data="faq-20",
        evaluators=[correctness],
        experiment_prefix=name,
        max_concurrency=4,
    )

options: Two new datasets named prompt-a and prompt-b
Two tracing projects with no scores, because evaluators need a separate call
Two experiments on the faq-20 dataset, each with 20 runs scored by correctness, which you can compare side by side
One experiment containing 40 runs mixed together
objective.explanation: Each evaluate() call creates its own experiment on the same dataset. experiment_prefix names it, and max_concurrency runs up to 4 examples in parallel. Evaluators run inside evaluate(), and no new datasets are created.

objective.question: You are doing the Week 7 hands-on task: comparing two prompts on a 20-example dataset. Which order of steps is correct?
options: Write the evaluators → run prompt A and prompt B in one evaluate() call → create the dataset → read only the averages

Create the dataset with 20 examples → write the target and evaluators → run evaluate() for prompt A → run evaluate() for prompt B with only the prompt changed → open both experiments in the comparison view
Create the dataset → change the prompt and the model together → run one experiment → compare it with last month's production traces
Run evaluate() for prompt A → create the dataset → write the evaluators → run prompt B → compare
objective.explanation: An experiment needs a dataset, a target and evaluators first. Then each prompt gets its own experiment on the same data, with one variable changed, and the comparison view shows per-example differences. The other orders either run before the data exists, mix variables, or skip the comparison.

objective.question: Your LangSmith workspace is in the EU region. LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY are set correctly, but no traces appear. The logs show authentication errors when the SDK sends runs. What is the most likely fix?
options: Set LANGSMITH_PROJECT to a new project name
Decorate the agent with @traceable so the key is used
Replace LANGSMITH_TRACING with LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2
Set LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT to the EU API URL so the SDK sends traces to the EU region
objective.explanation: By default the SDK sends traces to the US endpoint. An EU workspace key is rejected there, so you must point LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT to the EU API. A project name or @traceable does not change where the data is sent, and the legacy variable name does not fix a region mismatch.

objective.question: A code reviewer flags this langgraph.json. What is the best fix?
options: Remove the "env" field entirely; langgraph dev reads keys from LangSmith
Change "env" to ".env", put the keys in that file, and add .env to .gitignore
Base64-encode the keys inside "env"
Move the keys into the "graphs" block
objective.explanation: langgraph.json is committed to the repo, so you should not put secrets in it. The env field can reference an .env file, which stays out of version control. Encoding is not protection, and removing env leaves the server with no keys at all.

objective.question: You need one precision score and one recall score for the whole experiment, computed across all 20 examples, not an average of per-example scores. How do you do this with evaluate()?
options: Pass a function to summary_evaluators that receives lists of outputs and reference_outputs and returns one score
Set num_repetitions=20 on evaluate()
Run 20 separate evaluate() calls and average the results in a spreadsheet
Return a list of scores from a normal per-example evaluator
objective.explanation: Summary evaluators run once per experiment and get every example's outputs together, so they can compute dataset-level metrics such as precision, recall or F1. Per-example evaluators score one example at a time. Repetitions rerun the same examples and do not aggregate this way.

objective.question: Tracing works when you run the agent with langgraph dev. When you run `python run_eval.py`, nothing appears in LangSmith, but no errors are shown. The keys live in a .env file in the project root. What is the most likely cause?
options: evaluate() never creates traces
The .env file must be named langsmith.env
LangSmith blocks traces from scripts that are not deployed
The plain Python script never loads .env, so LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY are not in its environment
objective.explanation: langgraph dev loads the env file named in langgraph.json, but a plain Python process does not read .env on its own. Load it first, for example with python-dotenv's load_dotenv(), or export the variables in the shell. evaluate() does trace target runs.

objective.question: Prompt B gives answers that are clearly correct but phrased differently from the reference outputs. Its score drops from 0.75 to 0.40 compared with prompt A. The evaluator is `outputs["answer"].strip() == reference_outputs["answer"].strip()`. What is the best explanation and fix?
options: The dataset is corrupted; recreate it
Increase temperature so the wording matches more often
Exact match is too strict for free-text answers; use an LLM-as-judge correctness evaluator, or check for key facts, and then re-read a sample of scores
Prompt B is worse; ship prompt A
objective.explanation: Exact string match penalises correct paraphrases, so the score measures wording, not correctness. A judge or a key-fact check fits free-text answers better, but you should still spot-check its scores. Raising temperature only adds noise.

objective.question: This experiment shows an error on every example and no scores. What is wrong?
options: Evaluators must return a float, not a bool
agent.invoke must be given a thread_id for evaluate() to work
The target returns a message object, not its text, so .lower() fails; return result["messages"][-1].content
inputs should be read as inputs.question
objective.explanation: result["messages"][-1] is an AIMessage, which has no .lower() method, so the evaluator raises an error. Returning the message text fixes it. Bool return values are valid feedback, and a thread_id is only needed when the agent has a checkpointer.

objective.question: You run your create_agent graph under langgraph dev for Studio. In agent.py you compiled it with checkpointer=InMemorySaver(). What should you do?
options: Pass the checkpointer again in the Studio UI
Remove the custom checkpointer for the served graph, because the Agent Server handles persistence automatically
Replace it with a database checkpointer in langgraph.json
Keep it, because Studio cannot save threads without it
objective.explanation: When the graph runs on the Agent Server, which langgraph dev starts locally, persistence is handled for you. A hand-built InMemorySaver is not needed and can conflict with the server. Keep custom checkpointers for scripts that run the graph directly.

objective.question: You will run many prompt experiments this month. Later you must filter the experiments by prompt commit and model. Which call makes that easiest?
options: Copy the dataset to a new name, such as faq-20-prompt-b, for each run
Add the prompt commit as an extra input key on every example
Set LANGSMITH_PROJECT=prompt-b before each run
evaluate(target_b, data="faq-20", evaluators=[correctness], experiment_prefix="prompt-b", metadata={"prompt_commit": "a1b2c3", "model": MODEL})
objective.explanation: experiment_prefix gives each experiment a readable name, and metadata stores the prompt commit and model on the experiment, so you can filter and compare later. Copying datasets or changing inputs breaks like-for-like comparison, and LANGSMITH_PROJECT controls where traces go, not experiment labels.

objective.question: Your agent calls a custom internal LLM over raw HTTP inside a @traceable function. The run appears in the trace, but it shows no token counts and is not shown as an LLM call. What fixes this?
options: Wrap the function in a LangGraph node
Use @traceable(run_type="llm") and report the model's token usage in the run output, for example as usage_metadata
Tokens are only recorded for OpenAI models, so nothing can be done
Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=verbose
objective.explanation: LangSmith shows a run as an LLM call and records its tokens when the run is typed as an LLM and the usage is reported. A plain @traceable creates a generic chain run with no token data. There is no verbose tracing value, and a graph node does not add usage information.

objective.question: Halfway through evaluate() on your 20 examples, many target runs fail with HTTP 429 errors from the model provider. What is the first change to make?
options: Switch the evaluator to LLM-as-judge
Turn off LANGSMITH_TRACING
Lower max_concurrency in evaluate() and add retries, for example with tool or model retry middleware
Delete the failing examples from the dataset
objective.explanation: A 429 error means you hit the provider's rate limit. Running fewer examples in parallel, with retries, fixes it without changing what you measure. Deleting examples biases the experiment, and tracing or the choice of evaluator does not cause provider rate limits.

objective.question: The agent below is evaluated with evaluate(). It scores 0 on every 'send a refund email' example. The traces end right after the model proposes a send_email tool call. What is the cause and the best fix?
options: send_email should be removed from the dataset

The interrupt pauses the graph before the tool runs; in the target, detect the interrupt and resume on the same thread_id with Command(resume=...) carrying a fixed approve decision, or evaluate a variant without the HITL middleware
The thread_id must be the same for every example
The checkpointer is missing a store; add InMemoryStore()
objective.explanation: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses the graph for a human decision, so invoke returns before send_email runs and before the final answer exists. In offline evaluation the target must supply that decision by resuming on the same thread, or you test a variant without the pause. A shared thread_id would mix histories, and a store does not affect interrupts.

objective.question: Your dataset 'support-20' has a split named 'hard' with 6 examples. You want a quick experiment on just those 6. Which data argument is correct?
options: data=client.list_examples(dataset_name="support-20", splits=["hard"])
data="support-20", plus a filter inside the evaluator that returns None for other examples
data="support-20", plus num_repetitions=6
data="support-20/hard"
objective.explanation: evaluate() accepts an iterable of examples, and list_examples can filter by split. A path-style dataset name is not valid syntax. Filtering inside the evaluator still runs the target on all 20 examples, and repetitions do not select a subset.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between a trace and a run in LangSmith, using an agent request as an example.
subjective.answer: A run is one unit of work, such as one LLM call, one tool call, one retriever call or one decorated function. A trace is the full tree of runs for a single top-level request. For example, a user asks my create_agent support bot about an order. The root run is the agent invocation. Under it I see a model run that decides to call a tool, then the get_order tool run, then a second model run that writes the final answer. Each run has its own inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and errors. The trace ties them together with parent-child links, so I can see the order of events and which step caused a problem. When debugging, I start at the root run and drill into the child run where time, tokens or errors are concentrated.
keyPoints: A run is a single step: an LLM, tool, retriever or @traceable function
A trace is the tree of runs for one request, with a root run
Each run carries its own inputs, outputs, latency, tokens and errors
Debug by drilling from the root run into the failing or slow child run

subjective.question: How do you enable LangSmith tracing for a LangChain or LangGraph app, and how would you keep dev and prod traces separate?
subjective.answer: I set two environment variables: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY set to my key. Once these are set, LangChain and LangGraph code, including create_agent graphs, is traced automatically, with no code changes. To choose where traces go, I set LANGSMITH_PROJECT. Without it, traces land in the default project, which quickly gets messy. To separate environments, I use a different project name per environment, such as support-bot-dev and support-bot-prod, set through each environment's config or secrets manager, never hard-coded. I keep the API key out of Git, for example in a .env file that is git-ignored locally and in a secret store in deployment. For my own helper functions that are not LangChain components, I add @traceable so they show up inside the same trace tree.
keyPoints: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY are the minimum
LANGSMITH_PROJECT selects the project; otherwise traces go to the default project
Use one project per environment, set via env vars
Keep keys in secrets, not code; use @traceable for custom functions

subjective.question: Users complain an agent sometimes gives a wrong answer after calling a tool. Walk through how you would use a trace to find the cause.
subjective.answer: I filter the project for the bad conversations, for example by user feedback, error status or a keyword, and open one trace. First, I read the model run's input messages to confirm the system prompt and user message were what I expected. Next, I check the tool call the model produced: the tool name and arguments. Often the bug is a wrong argument, like a malformed order ID. Then I open the tool run and check its actual output. If the tool returned correct data but the final model run misread it, the fix is in the prompt or the tool's output format. If the tool returned bad or empty data, the fix is in the tool or its arguments. I compare against a good trace for the same kind of question. Finally, I add the failing case to my dataset so the fix can be measured.
keyPoints: Locate bad traces through filters or feedback
Inspect prompts, tool-call names and arguments, then tool outputs
Decide whether the fault is in the prompt, the tool arguments or the tool itself
Compare with a good trace; add the failure to the dataset

subjective.question: How do latency and token metadata in a trace help you control cost and speed? Give concrete actions.
subjective.answer: Each LLM run in a trace records latency and token usage, split into input and output tokens, and the root run aggregates them. For speed, I look at which child run takes the most time. A slow tool points to caching, a timeout or a faster API. Several sequential model calls suggest the agent is looping, which I can cap with a model-call limit middleware. For cost, I check where input tokens grow. A long conversation history growing every turn suggests SummarizationMiddleware with a token trigger. A huge system prompt or verbose tool outputs suggest trimming prompts or returning only the fields the model needs. Large output tokens may mean the prompt invites long answers. I then re-run the dataset as an experiment to confirm the change cut tokens or latency without lowering quality scores.
keyPoints: Latency is per run; find the dominant child run
Tokens are split into input and output; track where input grows
Fixes include caching, call limits, summarization, trimming prompts and tool output
Verify the fix with an experiment so quality does not drop

subjective.question: You must build a 20-example dataset for a customer-support agent. How do you choose the examples and structure them?
subjective.answer: Each example has inputs, such as {"question": ...}, and, where possible, reference outputs such as {"answer": ...}. With only 20 examples, coverage matters more than volume. I would include roughly 10 common real questions taken from production traces, about 5 edge cases such as ambiguous questions, missing order IDs or multi-step requests, and about 5 known past failures or adversarial cases, for example out-of-scope or prompt-injection attempts. I write reference answers that state the key facts, not exact wording, so an LLM judge can grade correctness fairly. I keep the input keys consistent with what my target function reads. I can use metadata or splits to tag categories, so I can see where a prompt helps or hurts. I freeze this dataset while comparing prompts. If I add examples later, I rerun both prompts, so they are compared on the same data.
keyPoints: An example is inputs plus optional reference outputs
Mix common, edge-case and past-failure examples; source them from real traces
Reference outputs should capture key facts for fair judging
Keep keys consistent; tag categories; freeze the dataset during comparisons

subjective.question: When would you use a code-based evaluator versus an LLM-as-judge evaluator? Show what a simple code evaluator looks like.
subjective.answer: I use code evaluators when the check is objective and cheap: exact match, valid JSON, the correct tool called, an answer under a length limit, or a required field present. They are deterministic, fast and free. A code evaluator is a function with named arguments, for example def has_order_id(inputs, outputs, reference_outputs): return reference_outputs["order_id"] in outputs["answer"]. It can return a bool, a number, or a dict like {"key": "has_order_id", "score": 1}. I use an LLM-as-judge when quality is semantic, such as whether the answer is correct in meaning, helpful or grounded, and wording can vary. openevals gives create_llm_as_judge(prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, model=..., feedback_key="correctness"). Judges cost money and can be noisy, so I combine them: code checks for hard rules and a judge for meaning.
keyPoints: Code evaluators suit objective, deterministic checks
Arguments are matched by name: inputs, outputs, reference_outputs
Return a bool, a number, or a dict with key and score
Use an LLM judge for semantic quality; combine both types

subjective.question: Describe step by step how you ran the hands-on task: comparing two prompts on a 20-example dataset.
subjective.answer: First, I created the dataset in LangSmith with 20 examples, each with inputs {"question"} and reference outputs {"answer"}. Second, I wrote a target factory: a function that builds the agent with a given system_prompt and returns target(inputs) -> {"answer": ...}. The model, tools and settings were identical for both prompts. Third, I defined evaluators: an openevals create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT and feedback_key="correctness", plus a simple code evaluator for answer length. Fourth, I ran evaluate(target_a, data="support-20", evaluators=[...], experiment_prefix="prompt-a"), then the same call with target_b and experiment_prefix="prompt-b". Finally, I opened both experiments in the comparison view. I checked the average correctness and then each example where B scored lower or higher. I read those traces to confirm the change in scores matched the prompt change.
keyPoints: Same dataset, model, tools and evaluators; only the prompt differs
Target takes the inputs dict and returns an outputs dict
Use evaluate() with a distinct experiment_prefix per prompt
Use the comparison view for averages plus per-example diffs

subjective.question: Why should you change only one thing per experiment? What else can make a score difference misleading?
subjective.answer: If I change the prompt and the model together and the score rises, I cannot tell which change helped. One of them might even have hurt while the other helped more. Changing only one variable per experiment, with the same dataset, evaluators and model, lets me credit the difference to that change. Other things can still mislead. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, so a small gap on 20 examples may just be noise. I can run repetitions or check whether the gain is consistent across examples. The LLM judge is also noisy and can be biased, so I spot-check its grades. A small or unrepresentative dataset can reward overfitting to those examples. Averages can hide regressions on important cases. So I look at per-example changes, repeat runs when the gap is small, and grow the dataset over time.
keyPoints: One change per experiment gives clear attribution
LLM non-determinism means small gaps may be noise; repeat runs
LLM judges are noisy; spot-check their grades
Small datasets and averages can mislead; inspect per-example results

subjective.question: How do you make an LLM-as-judge evaluator trustworthy?
subjective.answer: I treat the judge as a model that also needs evaluation. First, I start from a tested prompt such as openevals' CORRECTNESS_PROMPT and give it reference outputs, so it grades against facts instead of its own opinion. Second, I give each judge one clear criterion and a named feedback_key, rather than one vague overall-quality score. Third, I calibrate it. I hand-label a sample of outputs, compare them with the judge's scores, and read its reasoning where they disagree. If it is too lenient or too strict, I adjust the rubric. Fourth, I keep the judge model fixed across the experiments I compare. Changing the judge changes the measuring tool. I also prefer a strong model for judging, and I back the judge with code evaluators for objective rules. I keep monitoring for drift as the product changes.
keyPoints: Use a proven prompt and reference outputs
Use one criterion per judge, with a clear feedback_key
Calibrate against human labels and review disagreements
Keep the judge model fixed across compared experiments

subjective.question: What is prompt versioning in LangSmith and why does it matter for agent teams?
subjective.answer: Prompt versioning means storing prompts in LangSmith's prompt management instead of only in code. Every saved change becomes a new version (a commit) that you can view, compare and roll back to, and you can mark particular versions with tags. The app then pulls a prompt by name, or by a specific version or tag. This matters for three reasons. First, traceability: when an experiment improves, I know exactly which prompt version produced it. Second, safe rollout: I can promote a version through dev and prod by moving a tag, and roll back quickly if production traces show regressions. Third, collaboration: product people can edit and test prompts in the UI or playground without a code deploy. The discipline is to run a dataset experiment before promoting any new version, so each version change is backed by a score.
keyPoints: Prompts are stored centrally, with each change saved as a version
Pull prompts by name or by a specific version or tag
Links experiment results to exact prompt versions; supports rollback
Gate every version promotion with a dataset experiment

subjective.question: How do you set up LangSmith Studio to debug a LangGraph agent locally, and what does it give you?
subjective.answer: I add a langgraph.json at the project root. It lists the dependencies, the graphs mapping a name to the module and variable, such as "agent": "./src/agent.py:agent", and the env file holding my keys. The graph can be a StateGraph I compiled myself or the graph returned by create_agent. Then I install the LangGraph CLI and run langgraph dev, which starts a local server, and I connect Studio to it. I don't attach my own checkpointer in this setup, because the server handles persistence. Studio gives me a visual view of the graph's nodes and edges. I can send inputs, watch state change node by node, inspect threads and checkpoints, and resume interrupts such as human-in-the-loop approvals. I can also edit state and re-run from an earlier step. Runs are traced to LangSmith, so I move from debugging straight to traces and datasets.
keyPoints: langgraph.json declares dependencies, graphs and env
Start the local server with langgraph dev and connect Studio
The server handles persistence, so no custom checkpointer is needed
Visualise the graph, inspect state and threads, handle interrupts and re-run steps

subjective.question: Checkpoint: how would you convince a reviewer that your score improved because of your change and not by chance?
subjective.answer: I would show two experiments on the same frozen 20-example dataset, with the same model and the same evaluators, differing only in the system prompt. I would name the prompt version used in each. Then I open the comparison view. For example, correctness rose from 0.65 to 0.85. I would show which examples flipped from fail to pass and open their traces, to show that the new instruction directly changed the behaviour, such as asking for a missing order ID instead of guessing. I would also show whether any example regressed and explain it. To rule out noise, I would re-run each prompt, or use repetitions, and show the gain holds. I would also spot-check a few judge grades against my own reading. This gives a reproducible, attributable result rather than a single lucky number.
keyPoints: Experiments share the same dataset, model and evaluators; only the prompt differs
Use the comparison view to show which examples flipped, with supporting traces
Report regressions honestly
Repeat runs and spot-check the judge to rule out noise

subjective.question: Explain what this code does, and suggest two improvements before you use the dataset to compare prompts.

code.code:
from langsmith import Client

client = Client()
ds = client.create_dataset(
    dataset_name="faq-20",
    description="Support FAQ questions with expected answers",
)
client.create_examples(
    dataset_id=ds.id,
    examples=[
        {"inputs": {"question": "How do I reset my password?"},
         "outputs": {"answer": "Use 'Forgot password' on the login page."}},
        # ... 19 more
    ],
)

subjective.answer: The code creates a LangSmith client using LANGSMITH_API_KEY. It creates a dataset called faq-20 and adds examples to it. Each example has inputs, which become the target function's input, and outputs, which evaluators receive as reference_outputs. Two improvements. First, add metadata to each example, such as category ('billing', 'account') or difficulty ('edge case'). Then you can slice experiment results and see where prompt B wins or loses. Second, make the set representative and stable. Include hard and adversarial cases, out-of-scope questions where the right answer is a refusal, and questions that need a tool call. Do not edit the examples between the prompt A and prompt B runs. If you must change them, create a new dataset version so the comparison stays fair. Guarding the create call so reruns do not fail or duplicate the dataset also helps.
keyPoints: inputs feed the target; outputs become reference_outputs
Add per-example metadata to slice results
Cover edge, refusal and tool-use cases
Keep the dataset fixed or versioned across compared experiments

subjective.question: Your agent handles customer emails and phone numbers. Security says raw PII must not be stored in LangSmith traces. What options do you have, and which would you choose?
subjective.answer: I would protect the data at two layers. At the agent layer, PIIMiddleware from langchain.agents.middleware can redact PII before it reaches the model. An example is PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True), plus a similar rule for phone numbers. The model and the traced model calls then see redacted text, which also lowers the risk of the model leaking data. At the tracing layer, LangSmith can hide inputs and outputs. The LANGSMITH_HIDE_INPUTS and LANGSMITH_HIDE_OUTPUTS settings work for all runs, and the SDK also lets you mask fields selectively. Hiding everything costs you debugging value, so I prefer targeted redaction. I would also use separate projects for prod and dev, give LangSmith access only to the people who need it, and never copy raw production traces into datasets without redacting them first. Finally, I would check a few traces by hand to confirm that no PII remains.
keyPoints: PIIMiddleware redacts before the model sees data
LangSmith can hide or mask trace inputs and outputs
Trade-off between privacy and debuggability
Redact before turning prod traces into datasets; verify manually

subjective.question: Your agent's final answers score well, but you suspect it calls the wrong tools or calls tools too often. How would you evaluate the agent's trajectory, not just its final answer?
subjective.answer: Final-answer correctness can hide bad behaviour. For example, the agent might call search_orders three times, or guess without calling any tool at all. To evaluate the trajectory, I make the target return the full message list from the create_agent graph, not just the last message. In the dataset, I add reference outputs such as the expected tool names, for example ["lookup_customer", "search_orders"]. Then I write a code evaluator. It walks the AI messages, collects the tool_calls names, and scores two things: whether the required tools were called in a sensible order, and whether the number of calls stays under a limit. I log these as separate feedback keys, such as tool_choice and tool_calls_count, next to correctness. For subtler judgements, an LLM-as-judge can grade whether each tool call was justified. When I compare experiments, I look at trajectory scores together with tokens and latency from the traces.
keyPoints: Return full messages from the target, not just final text
Store expected tools as reference outputs
Code evaluator over tool_calls: right tools, order, count
Separate feedback keys alongside correctness

subjective.question: Prompt B raised correctness from 0.70 to 0.85 on your 20-example dataset, but median latency rose 60% and tokens per run doubled. How do you decide whether to ship it?
subjective.answer: I treat this as a trade-off decision, not an automatic win. First, I check that the gain is real. I compare the two experiments example by example, look at which examples flipped, and rerun with repetitions to rule out noise. Next, I use the traces to find where the cost comes from. A longer system prompt, extra reasoning, or additional tool calls would each point to a different fix. Then I put the numbers in business terms: the cost per 1,000 requests, and whether the new latency still meets our response-time target. If the correctness gain covers high-value cases such as refunds, it may be worth paying for. After that, I try to keep the quality while cutting the cost. I can trim the prompt or move rarely used instructions into tool descriptions, then run another experiment that changes only one thing. I would ship once both quality and budget thresholds pass, or ship behind a flag to a small share of traffic first.
keyPoints: Verify the gain per example and with repetitions
Use traces to locate token and latency increases
Translate into cost and SLA terms
Iterate one change at a time; staged rollout

subjective.question: How would you turn your prompt comparison into a regression check that runs in CI before every deploy?
subjective.answer: I would write a script that the CI pipeline runs on each pull request. It sets LANGSMITH_API_KEY from CI secrets, turns tracing on, and points LANGSMITH_PROJECT at a CI-specific project. It calls evaluate() with the production target, the fixed regression dataset, and my evaluators. These include a cheap code evaluator such as exact match or tool choice, and an openevals LLM-as-judge for correctness. I give it an experiment_prefix that includes the git commit, so every run is traceable. After the run, the script reads the experiment results, computes the average for each feedback key, and fails the build if a score falls below a threshold. Comparing against the last main-branch experiment is better still. I keep the dataset small so the check stays fast and cheap, and I pin the judge model and prompt version so the scores stay comparable. When the check fails, reviewers open the experiment in LangSmith and inspect the failing examples' traces.
keyPoints: CI runs evaluate() with secrets and a CI project
experiment_prefix tied to commit
Threshold or baseline comparison fails the build
Pin judge model and prompt versions; keep the dataset small

subjective.question: Explain what this evaluation target does and why each part matters.
subjective.answer: The code builds a LangChain v1 agent with create_agent. It uses one tool and prompt B as the system prompt, and it returns a compiled LangGraph graph. The target function is what evaluate() calls for each example. LangSmith passes in the example's inputs dict, so inputs["question"] must match the dataset schema. The function wraps the question as a user message, invokes the agent, and returns a dict whose "answer" key matches the reference outputs, so evaluators can compare like with like. The agent is created once, outside the function, so the runs share the same setup and do not rebuild it each time. To compare prompts fairly, prompt A's target must be identical except for system_prompt. Every invocation is traced under the experiment, so you can open any low-scoring example and see its tool calls. If you also want trajectory evaluation, return the full messages list as well. No checkpointer is needed, because each example is independent.
keyPoints: Target receives the example inputs dict
Output keys should align with reference outputs
Only system_prompt differs between compared targets
Each call is traced inside the experiment

subjective.question: Your offline dataset scores are high, yet users still report failures in production. How would you use production traces to improve your dataset and evaluations?
subjective.answer: High offline scores with production failures usually mean the dataset does not reflect real traffic. First, I filter production traces in LangSmith using negative user feedback, errors, long latency, or metadata such as tier or category. I read those traces to find the patterns, for example a tool that returns empty results, or questions phrased in an unexpected way. I then add the representative failing runs to the dataset as new examples. I redact any PII, and I write a correct reference output by hand, because the agent's own wrong output must not become the reference. I tag these examples with metadata like source=prod and their category. Then I rerun the current prompt to confirm the new examples fail, so the dataset now catches the problem. Only after that do I make a fix and run a new experiment. Over time, the dataset becomes a growing regression suite drawn from real failures. I keep a fixed core subset so I can still compare scores across time.
keyPoints: Filter prod traces by feedback, errors, metadata
Add failing runs as examples with corrected references
Redact PII; tag source and category
Confirm examples fail before fixing; keep a stable core

subjective.question: Case study: you have two weeks to ship an FAQ agent built with create_agent. Requirements: every run is traced, dev and prod traces stay separate, you can show that a prompt change improved quality, engineers can debug locally, and no secrets go into the repo. Outline your plan.
subjective.answer: First, tracing. I set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY in an .env file listed in .gitignore. I set LANGSMITH_PROJECT to faq-dev locally and faq-prod in the deployed environment. Second, local debugging. I add a langgraph.json whose graphs entry points to the agent and whose env field is ".env", then run langgraph dev and use Studio. Third, data. I build a 20-example dataset from real FAQ questions, with reference answers and a few edge cases, and I tag the dataset version. Fourth, evaluation. I write a target that returns a dict, plus an openevals correctness judge and one cheap code check, such as refusing out-of-scope questions. I run prompt A as a baseline, then prompt B with only the prompt changed, and I record the prompt commit in metadata. Finally, I compare both experiments per example, spot-check the judge's scores, and ship the winning prompt by its pinned version.
keyPoints: Secrets in .env, never in code or langgraph.json
LANGSMITH_PROJECT per environment
langgraph.json with env pointing to .env, for Studio
Tagged dataset, baseline experiment, one-variable change
Per-example comparison and judge spot-checks before shipping

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this evaluation script. It is meant to compare prompt A and prompt B.

code.code:
from langsmith import evaluate
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

def make_target(prompt, temp):
    model = init_chat_model(MODEL, temperature=temp)
    agent = create_agent(model, tools=tools, system_prompt=prompt)
    def target(inputs):
        r = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": inputs["question"]}]})
        return r["messages"][-1].content
    return target

def correct(outputs, reference_outputs):
    return reference_outputs["answer"].lower() in outputs["answer"].lower()

evaluate(make_target(PROMPT_A, 0.0), data="faq-20", evaluators=[correct])
evaluate(make_target(PROMPT_B, 0.7), data="faq-20", evaluators=[correct])

subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, the target returns a plain string, but the evaluator reads outputs["answer"], so scoring breaks. The target should return {"answer": r["messages"][-1].content}. Second, the two runs change both the prompt and the temperature. If the score moves, you cannot say which change caused it. Keep the temperature fixed, ideally 0, and change only the prompt. Third, neither run has an experiment_prefix or metadata, so the experiments get auto-generated names. Later you will not know which one was prompt B or which prompt version it used. Add experiment_prefix="prompt-a" and "prompt-b", plus metadata with the prompt commit. Fourth, the evaluator checks whether the whole reference answer appears inside the output. That only rewards near-verbatim answers, so correct paraphrases score 0. Use key facts or an LLM-as-judge instead, and spot-check the results.
keyPoints: Target must return a dict with the key the evaluator reads
Two variables changed (prompt and temperature)
No experiment_prefix or metadata for traceability
Substring match is too strict for free text

subjective.question: Compare absolute scoring (each answer gets a correctness score) with pairwise comparison (a judge picks the better of two answers). When is each the better choice for comparing prompt A and prompt B?
subjective.answer: Absolute scoring gives every answer its own score, such as correct or incorrect, or a value from 0 to 1. It works well when there is a clear reference answer or a clear rule. Scores are stable over time, so you can track a baseline across many experiments and use them in CI. Its weakness is subtle quality differences. If both prompts are 'correct', absolute scores can tie even when one answer is clearly clearer or more complete. Pairwise comparison asks a judge which of two answers is better for the same input. It is more sensitive to differences in tone, completeness and helpfulness, and it does not need a perfect reference. But the result only holds for that pair, and judges can prefer whichever answer is shown first, so run both orders. I use absolute scoring as the main gate, and pairwise when scores tie and I need to choose on quality.
keyPoints: Absolute: needs a reference or rule; stable; good for regression and CI
Pairwise: sensitive to subtle quality; no perfect reference needed
Pairwise results are relative to one pair; watch position bias
Combine them: absolute as the gate, pairwise to break ties

subjective.question: Put in order the steps to debug, in LangSmith Studio, a LangGraph agent that picks the wrong tool, and explain each step.
subjective.answer: 1. Check that langgraph.json points to the compiled graph, such as ./src/agent.py:graph, has its dependencies listed, and references .env through the env field. 2. Run langgraph dev. This starts a local Agent Server and gives a Studio link. 3. In Studio, select the graph and send the failing user input on a new thread. 4. Watch the graph run step by step. Open the model step and read the exact messages and the tool call it produced, including the tool name and arguments. 5. Look at the state before that step. Are the system prompt, tool descriptions and earlier messages what you expected? 6. Make a fix, such as a clearer tool description or prompt. The dev server reloads on code changes. You can also edit the state and re-run from an earlier checkpoint to test a hypothesis. 7. Confirm the fix in Studio. Then add this input to your dataset and rerun the experiment, so the bug cannot come back unnoticed.
keyPoints: Correct langgraph.json, then langgraph dev
Reproduce on a fresh thread in Studio
Inspect the model step's messages and the tool-call arguments
Edit state or code and re-run from a checkpoint
Add the case to the dataset as a regression example

subjective.question: This is failing: the fetch calls show up in LangSmith as separate root traces instead of as children of handle_query. What is the cause, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: LangSmith links a child run to its parent through the current run context. That context is stored in Python context variables. A plain ThreadPoolExecutor starts work in new threads, and those threads do not inherit that context. So each fetch call finds no parent and starts its own root trace. The tree breaks, and the latency of handle_query looks wrong because its children are missing. The fix is to propagate the context into the threads. LangSmith provides ContextThreadPoolExecutor in langsmith.utils, which is a drop-in replacement that copies the context. Another option is to pass the parent run explicitly through the langsmith_extra argument. After the fix, the fetch runs appear nested under handle_query, and the parallel timing shows clearly in the trace. The same problem can appear with other manual thread or process setups, so check the trace tree whenever you add concurrency.
keyPoints: Parent-child linking relies on context variables
Plain threads do not inherit that context
Use ContextThreadPoolExecutor, or pass the parent explicitly
Check the trace tree after adding concurrency

subjective.question: Spot the mistake in this design: 'We wrote 20 examples, tuned the prompt for two days by rerunning the experiment on them, and got correctness from 0.60 to 0.95. We will report 0.95 as expected production quality.'
subjective.answer: The mistake is tuning and reporting on the same 20 examples. After many rounds, the prompt is fitted to these specific questions, including wording that only helps them. So 0.95 is an optimistic, overfitted number, not an estimate of production quality. Twenty examples is also a small sample, so each example moves the score by 5 points. To fix it, split the data. Keep a development split for tuning, and hold back a separate test split that you run only once, at the end. Use dataset splits in LangSmith for this. Report the held-out score, show the per-example comparison, and spot-check the judge. Also add fresh examples taken from real production traces, because a dataset written by the team often misses the messy inputs that real users send. Then treat that final score as the baseline to watch in production.
keyPoints: Tuning and reporting on the same data causes overfitting
Twenty examples is a small, noisy sample
Use dev and held-out test splits
Add real production examples; report the held-out score

subjective.question: For a policy Q&A agent, which reference output style is better: full model answers, or a short list of key facts the answer must contain? Explain the trade-off.
subjective.answer: For most agent work, I prefer key facts, sometimes with a short reference answer as context. A full reference answer pushes evaluators toward judging style. An LLM judge may mark a correct answer down because its structure differs, and string checks fail on paraphrases. Key facts, such as 'refund within 14 days' and 'must keep the receipt', state what correctness means. They are easier to write consistently across 20 examples and easier to audit. They also allow both a simple code evaluator (are the facts present?) and a judge prompt that checks them. Full answers still help when tone, format or completeness matter, for example a required email template, or when you run pairwise comparisons. The risk with key facts is missing a requirement, such as an answer that adds wrong extra claims. So I add a 'must not say' list or a hallucination check for that.
keyPoints: Full answers bias scoring toward wording
Key facts define correctness clearly and are easy to audit
Key facts support both code checks and judge rubrics
Add 'must not say' checks so wrong extra claims are caught

subjective.question: Your openevals correctness judge gives almost every answer a full score, including some you know are wrong. What could be causing this, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: First, I would check that the judge receives reference_outputs. If the wrapper only passes inputs and outputs, the judge has no ground truth and tends to accept anything plausible. Second, the judge prompt may be too lenient. Add a clear rubric, ask for reasoning before the score, and say that any wrong fact means a failing score.
