Third, the judge model may be weak, or the same model that wrote the answers, which tends to approve its own style. A stronger or different judge model helps. Fourth, the score scale may be too coarse. To test the fix, I build a small calibration set of known good and known bad answers, check that the judge separates them, and read its explanations for a few high and low scores. Only after the judge agrees with my own labels do I trust its averages in experiments.
keyPoints: Make sure reference_outputs reach the judge
Write a stricter rubric and ask for reasoning first
Use a strong judge, ideally a different model from the agent
Calibrate on known good and bad answers and read explanations

subjective.question: You added SummarizationMiddleware(model=..., trigger=("tokens", 4000), keep=("messages", 20)) to a long-chat agent. Average tokens per request dropped, but a few requests are now much slower. How do you use traces to explain this?

code.code:
agent = create_agent(
    model,
    tools=tools,
    system_prompt=PROMPT,
    middleware=[SummarizationMiddleware(
        model=summary_model,
        trigger=("tokens", 4000),
        keep=("messages", 20),
    )],
    checkpointer=checkpointer,
)

subjective.answer: First, filter the traces to the slow requests and open their run trees. On those requests, I expect an extra LLM call before the main model call: the summarization step, which runs only when the history passes 4,000 tokens. Its run shows its own latency and token count, and it reads a large history, so it can add seconds. Fast requests have no such run because the trigger did not fire. I would confirm this by comparing a slow trace with a fast one on the same thread. The trade-off is then clear. A summary once in a while costs latency, but every later call is shorter and cheaper. To fix it, I can use a faster or cheaper summary model, tune the trigger and keep settings, or accept the occasional slow turn. I would then check the change with latency and token metrics, plus a quality evaluation, so the summaries do not lose facts.
keyPoints: Slow traces contain an extra summarization LLM run
The trigger only fires above the token threshold
Compare slow and fast traces on the same thread
Tune the summary model and the trigger/keep settings; re-check quality

subjective.question: Review this langgraph.json and project setup. List every problem you see and the fix for each.
subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, the graph path names a variable called agent, but the file defines graph, so the server cannot load it. It should be "./src/agent.py:graph". Second, there is no dependencies field. Without something like ["."] or a requirements reference, the server may not install or find your package and its imports. Third, a real API key is written in env. This file is committed, so the secret leaks. Use "env": ".env", keep the keys in .env, and add that file to .gitignore. The .env file should also hold LANGSMITH_API_KEY, so Studio runs are traced. Fourth, the graph is compiled with its own InMemorySaver. Under the Agent Server, which langgraph dev starts, persistence is handled automatically, so the custom checkpointer should be removed for the served graph. Keep it only for scripts that run the graph directly. After these fixes, langgraph dev should start cleanly and Studio can load threads.
keyPoints: Graph path must match the variable name (graph)
Add a dependencies field
Reference .env instead of inline secrets
Remove the custom checkpointer when served by the Agent Server

subjective.question: Describe, in order, how you would promote a new support prompt version to production using LangSmith prompt versioning and experiments.
subjective.answer: 1. Push the candidate prompt to LangSmith. Every push creates a new commit, so the text is versioned and you can see the differences. 2. Note the commit hash of the current production prompt, which is your baseline, and the hash of the candidate. 3. Run an experiment for each commit on the same dataset version, with the same model and temperature. Pull each prompt by its exact commit, and record the hash in the experiment metadata. 4. Compare the two experiments per example. Check correctness and any safety checks, and look at latency and tokens. Read the examples that regressed. 5. If the candidate wins, move the production tag to that commit, or update the app config to the new hash. Do this through your normal review process. 6. In production, the app should pull the prompt by tag or commit, never 'whatever is latest'. 7. After release, watch production traces and feedback. If quality drops, roll back by moving the tag to the old commit.
keyPoints: Every push creates a commit; compare by commit hash
Equal experiments with metadata recording the commit
Per-example comparison, plus latency and token checks
Promote via a tag or pinned commit, never 'latest'
Monitor after release; roll back by moving the tag

subjective.question: Your regression dataset grew from 20 to 500 examples. Each experiment now takes 40 minutes and costs a lot in judge calls. How do you keep evaluation fast without losing coverage?
subjective.answer: I split the work into tiers. A small smoke split, for example the original 20 examples plus the known hard cases, runs on every pull request. The full 500 runs nightly or before a release. I use dataset splits to tag examples by topic and difficulty, so I can run a focused subset when I change one area. For cost, I use cheap code evaluators first, such as format, required keywords or the expected tool name, and keep the LLM judge for the metrics that need it. I may also use a cheaper judge model, after checking it still agrees with my own labels. I remove near-duplicate examples that add cost but no new information. For speed, I tune max_concurrency to the highest level the provider's rate limits allow. I keep every dataset version tagged, so the smoke and full results stay comparable over time, and I watch per-split scores, not one global average.
keyPoints: Tiered runs: smoke split per PR, full set nightly or per release
Splits by topic and difficulty for focused runs
Cheap code evaluators first; judge only where needed
Remove near-duplicates; tune max_concurrency within rate limits
Tag dataset versions; report per-split scores

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: experiment A (last Monday) scored 0.72 and experiment B (today) scored 0.84 on 'faq-20'. A colleague says someone edited and added examples to the dataset on Wednesday. What is wrong with the comparison, and how do you fix it and prevent it?
subjective.answer: The two experiments may not have run on the same examples. If examples were added, removed or had their reference outputs changed, part of the 0.12 gain may come from the data, not from prompt B. Easier new examples or corrected references can raise the score by themselves. The comparison is not like-for-like. To fix it, I rerun both prompts now on the same dataset version. The cleanest way is to run prompt A again, because the model may also have drifted since Monday. LangSmith versions datasets, so I can also select examples as of a specific version, for example with list_examples using as_of, and pass them as data. To prevent it, I tag the dataset version used for each baseline, record it in the experiment metadata, and agree that dataset edits create a new version and a new baseline. Then every score gain can be explained by a single change.
keyPoints: The dataset changed between runs, so the comparison is not like-for-like
Rerun both prompts on the same dataset version
Use dataset version tags or as_of to pin the examples
Record the dataset version in metadata; edits mean a new baseline

steps.overview: This step takes the agent you built and evaluated and turns it into a running service. You describe it in langgraph.json, run it locally with the LangGraph CLI (`langgraph dev`) and debug it in LangSmith Studio. You then ship it to LangSmith Deployment, where it runs on Agent Server, stream answers into a web app and watch cost, latency and errors in production. Interviewers expect you to explain this path from a local graph to a monitored public endpoint.
objectives: Write a valid langgraph.json that points the Agent Server at your compiled graph, dependencies and environment file
Run the agent locally with `langgraph dev` and inspect, step through and re-run it in LangSmith Studio
Deploy the agent from a GitHub repository to LangSmith Deployment and get its public API URL
Stream tokens from the deployed agent into a web app through a backend proxy using the LangGraph SDK
Monitor latency, token cost and error rate of production traffic in LangSmith and act on regressions

concepts.explanation: This is the config file the CLI and Agent Server read to find and run your agent. Key fields are "dependencies" (for example ["."] to install your package), "graphs" (a map from graph ID to "./path/file.py:variable") and "env" (a path to a .env file). Optional fields include python_version, dockerfile_lines, store, checkpointer, http and auth. The graph ID you choose here becomes the assistant_id clients call.

Install it with `pip install -U "langgraph-cli[inmem]"`. `langgraph dev` starts a lightweight in-memory Agent Server with hot reload, so no Docker is needed. `langgraph build` produces a Docker image, and `langgraph up` runs the server in Docker with Postgres and Redis. `langgraph new` scaffolds a project from a template.

Studio is the visual agent IDE in LangSmith. It connects to a server started by `langgraph dev`. You can view the graph, send inputs, watch state at each node, handle interrupts, fork from earlier checkpoints and open traces. It talks to your local server through the baseUrl in the Studio link the CLI prints.

Agent Server (formerly LangGraph Server) is the runtime that serves your graph over an HTTP API. It exposes assistants, threads, runs (stateless or on a thread, streaming or background) and a long-term store. Persistence is automatic, so you do not pass your own checkpointer when you deploy. Remember that only the outermost graph is persisted.

This is the managed hosting option, formerly called LangGraph Platform or Cloud. You connect a GitHub repo that contains langgraph.json, choose a deployment type (development or production) and set secrets as environment variables. LangSmith then builds and runs Agent Server for you and gives you an API URL. Tracing to a LangSmith project is wired in automatically.

An assistant is a graph plus its configuration, and the default assistant ID equals the graph ID in langgraph.json. A thread holds the checkpointed state of one conversation. A run is a single execution of an assistant, optionally on a thread. Reusing a thread_id gives you memory across turns and lets you resume an interrupt with Command(resume=...).

The Python `langgraph_sdk` (`get_client`) and the JS `@langchain/langgraph-sdk` (including the React `useStream` hook) call Agent Server. `client.runs.stream(thread_id, assistant_id, input=..., stream_mode=...)` returns server-sent events. Use "messages-tuple" for LLM tokens, "updates" for per-node deltas and "values" for full state.

Every deployed run is traced to a LangSmith project. The monitoring dashboards chart trace volume, latency percentiles (P50/P99), error rate, token usage and cost over time. You can filter traces by metadata, add alerts and attach online evaluators to sample live traffic. Failed runs are found by filtering on error status and opening the trace.

keyFacts: Minimal langgraph.json: {"dependencies": ["."], "graphs": {"agent": "./src/agent/graph.py:graph"}, "env": ".env"}.
The "graphs" value must point to a compiled graph variable (such as the result of create_agent or StateGraph.compile()) or to a factory function, never to an uncompiled builder.
`langgraph dev` serves on http://127.0.0.1:2024 by default, keeps state in memory and hot-reloads on code changes; interactive API docs are at /docs.
`langgraph dev` is for development only; `langgraph up` and `langgraph build` use Docker, with Postgres for persistence and Redis for streaming and the task queue.
Do not compile your graph with your own checkpointer for deployment; Agent Server supplies persistence automatically.
The assistant_id you call equals the graph ID key in langgraph.json unless you create extra assistants.
Deployed endpoints are authenticated by default: send your LangSmith API key in the x-api-key header, or add custom auth via the "auth" field in langgraph.json.
Never ship the LangSmith API key to the browser; proxy calls through your backend or use custom auth.
Use stream_mode="messages-tuple" for token-by-token chat UX and "updates" when you want node-level progress.
Production tracing is automatic on LangSmith Deployment; locally, set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY.

example.caption: FastAPI proxy that streams tokens from a deployed agent to a browser (server-side key, public URL)
example.code:
# pip install fastapi uvicorn langgraph-sdk
import os, json
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from langgraph_sdk import get_client

client = get_client(
    url=os.environ["AGENT_URL"],            # deployment API URL from LangSmith
    api_key=os.environ["LANGSMITH_API_KEY"],  # stays on the server
)
app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/chat/{thread_id}")
async def chat(thread_id: str, body: dict):
    async def gen():
        async for chunk in client.runs.stream(
            thread_id, "agent",  # assistant_id = graph ID in langgraph.json
            input={"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": body["text"]}]},
            stream_mode="messages-tuple",
            if_not_exists="create",
        ):
            if chunk.event == "messages":
                msg, meta = chunk.data
                if msg.get("type") == "AIMessageChunk" and msg.get("content"):
                    yield f"data: {json.dumps(msg['content'])}\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")

# run: uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

pitfalls: Pointing "graphs" at the StateGraph builder instead of the compiled graph, or using a wrong module path. The server then fails to load the graph at startup.
Compiling with InMemorySaver for deployment. It is unnecessary, because Agent Server persists state automatically, and it can conflict with the platform's persistence.
Forgetting to add secrets such as model API keys as deployment environment variables. A local .env is not uploaded the way you might expect, so the deployed agent fails on its first model call.
Calling the deployment straight from frontend JavaScript with the LangSmith API key embedded. This leaks the key; use a backend proxy or custom auth.
Creating a new thread on every message, then wondering why the agent has no memory. Reuse the same thread_id for a conversation.
Treating `langgraph dev` as production. It is in-memory and single-process, so data is lost on restart.

workflow.title: From local agent to monitored public endpoint

steps.label: Write langgraph.json
steps.detail: Declare dependencies, map a graph ID to your compiled agent variable, and reference your .env file.

steps.label: Run langgraph dev

project.title: support-agent-deploy
project.summary: A small order-support agent built with LangChain v1 create_agent. You run it locally with the LangGraph CLI, open it in LangSmith Studio, deploy it with LangSmith Deployment, and stream its answers into a FastAPI web page through the LangGraph SDK. langgraph.json and pyproject.toml tell the Agent Server what to load, src/support_agent/agent.py is the graph, web/app.py and web/index.html are the streaming client, .env.example lists the secrets, and README.md covers the CLI, Studio, deployment and monitoring steps.
project.run:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e . "langgraph-cli[inmem]"
cp .env.example .env   # then fill in your keys
langgraph dev          # Agent Server on http://127.0.0.1:2024; Studio opens in the browser
AGENT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:2024 uvicorn web.app:app --port 8000   # second terminal; open http://localhost:8000

files.code:
# Installed by the Agent Server because langgraph.json lists dependencies: ["."]
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=68"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "support-agent-deploy"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
  "langchain>=1.0",          # create_agent and middleware
  "langchain-openai>=1.0",   # provider for "openai:..." model strings
  "langgraph-sdk",           # client used by the web app
  "fastapi",
  "uvicorn",
]

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src", "."]
include = ["support_agent*", "web*"]

# Copy to .env. Never commit the real .env file.

# Model provider key, used by the agent
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

# LangSmith tracing. Traces feed the Monitoring dashboards (cost, latency, errors).
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=lsv2_...
LANGSMITH_PROJECT=support-agent-deploy

# Used by web/app.py only.
# Local: http://127.0.0.1:2024
# Deployed: the API URL shown on your LangSmith Deployment page
AGENT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:2024

"""Order-support agent. The Agent Server imports `graph` from this file."""
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import PIIMiddleware, SummarizationMiddleware
from langchain.tools import tool

# Fake data so the sample runs with no database.
ORDERS = {
    "A100": {"status": "shipped", "eta": "2 days"},
    "A101": {"status": "processing", "eta": "5 days"},
}


@tool
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up the status and delivery estimate of an order by its ID."""
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id.upper())
    if order is None:
        return f"No order found with ID {order_id}."
    return f"Order {order_id}: {order['status']}, arriving in {order['eta']}."


# create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph.
# Do NOT pass a checkpointer here: the Agent Server adds persistence
# automatically, so threads keep their history across runs.
graph = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1-mini",
    tools=[get_order_status],
    system_prompt=(
        "You are a polite support agent for an online shop. "
        "Use get_order_status for any order question. Keep answers short."
    ),
    middleware=[
        # Hide customer emails before they reach the model and the traces.
        PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True),
        # Summarise long threads to control token cost in production.
        SummarizationMiddleware(
            model="openai:gpt-4.1-mini",
            trigger=("tokens", 4000),
            keep=("messages", 20),
        ),
    ],
)

"""FastAPI front end that streams tokens from the agent (local or deployed)."""
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import FileResponse, StreamingResponse
from langgraph_sdk import get_client
from pydantic import BaseModel

AGENT_URL = os.environ.get("AGENT_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:2024")
# The API key is needed for a LangSmith Deployment; it is ignored by `langgraph dev`.
# Keep it on the server. Never send it to the browser.
client = get_client(url=AGENT_URL, api_key=os.environ.get("LANGSMITH_API_KEY"))
ASSISTANT_ID = "agent"  # graph name from langgraph.json = default assistant

app = FastAPI()


class ChatIn(BaseModel):
    message: str
    thread_id: str | None = None  # the browser keeps this to continue a chat


@app.get("/")
def index():
    return FileResponse(Path(__file__).parent / "index.html")


@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(body: ChatIn):
    # A thread holds conversation state on the Agent Server.
    thread_id = body.thread_id or (await client.threads.create())["thread_id"]

    async def events():
        yield json.dumps({"thread_id": thread_id}) + "\n"
        # Each call to runs.stream starts one run on the thread.
        async for chunk in client.runs.stream(
            thread_id,
            ASSISTANT_ID,
            input={"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": body.message}]},
            stream_mode="messages-tuple",  # token-by-token LLM output
            metadata={"source": "web"},    # lets you filter these runs in LangSmith
        ):
            if chunk.event == "messages":
                msg, _meta = chunk.data
                # Send only AI text; skip tool messages and tool-call chunks.
                if msg.get("type") == "AIMessageChunk" and isinstance(msg.get("content"), str):
                    if msg["content"]:
                        yield json.dumps({"token": msg["content"]}) + "\n"
            elif chunk.event == "error":
                yield json.dumps({"error": str(chunk.data)}) + "\n"

    # Newline-delimited JSON. The browser reads it with fetch() and a stream reader.
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="application/x-ndjson")
Order support

# support-agent-deploy (Step 7: Deploy)

## 1. Run locally with the CLI
```
pip install -e . "langgraph-cli[inmem]"
cp .env.example .env    # add OPENAI_API_KEY and LANGSMITH_API_KEY
langgraph dev
```
`langgraph dev` reads `langgraph.json`. It starts an in-memory Agent Server on port 2024 and serves graph `agent`.

## 2. Open in LangSmith Studio
Studio opens automatically. You can also open:
`https://smith.langchain.com/studio/?baseUrl=http://127.0.0.1:2024`
Ask "Where is order A100?". Watch the tool call. Then open the thread and check its history.

## 3. Stream into the web app
```
uvicorn web.app:app --port 8000
```
Open http://localhost:8000. Tokens arrive through `client.runs.stream(..., stream_mode="messages-tuple")`.

## 4. Deploy with LangSmith Deployment
1. Push this repo to GitHub. Do not push `.env`.
2. In LangSmith, go to Deployments > New Deployment and connect the repo. The config file is `langgraph.json`.
3. Add `OPENAI_API_KEY` as a secret, then deploy.
4. Copy the deployment API URL. Set `AGENT_URL` to that URL and `LANGSMITH_API_KEY` to your key.
5. Host `web/app.py` on any public host (Render, Railway, Cloud Run, etc.) with those env vars set.

Checkpoint: the public web URL streams answers from the deployed agent.

## Concepts
- **Assistant**: a graph plus its config. `agent` is the default assistant.
- **Thread**: stored conversation state. The server persists it, so no checkpointer is needed in code.
- **Run**: one execution on a thread.

## 5. Monitor in production
In LangSmith, open the tracing project for your deployment.
- Use the Monitoring tab to track latency (P50/P99), error rate and token cost over time.
- Filter runs by metadata `source = web`.
- Open failed runs to read the error trace.
- Set alerts on error rate or latency where your plan supports them.

revision.examFocus: LangChain Academy courses have no proctored exam, so 'exam' here means course quizzes, the checkpoint demo and the deployment questions asked in agent-engineering interviews. This step maps to the deployment material in the LangGraph and LangSmith courses: the langgraph.json config, the local CLI and Studio loop, Agent Server concepts (assistants, threads, runs), SDK streaming and production monitoring. Questions are usually scenario-based: something breaks after deploy, memory is lost, or a key leaks, and you must name the cause and the fix.

compare.difference: dev is a single-process, in-memory server with hot reload for local work. up and build use Docker images backed by Postgres and Redis, so state and queues survive restarts.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the question says local iteration, hot reload, debugging in Studio or 'no Docker'.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when the question needs durable state, a production-like run or a container image to self-host.

compare.difference: messages-tuple emits LLM tokens as they are generated. updates emits one event per node after it finishes, carrying that node's state change.
compare.chooseA: Pick it for a ChatGPT-style typing effect in a chat UI.
compare.chooseB: Pick it for a progress view such as 'searching… summarising…' or for debugging which node changed what.

compare.difference: A thread holds the conversation's checkpointed state, so reusing it gives memory. A new thread always starts empty.
compare.chooseA: Pick it for every follow-up message in the same conversation, and to resume after an interrupt.
compare.chooseB: Pick it only when a new conversation or new user session begins.

compare.b: Custom auth via the "auth" field in langgraph.json
compare.difference: A proxy keeps the LangSmith key on your server and forwards requests. Custom auth lets end users call the deployment with their own tokens, which your auth handler validates.
compare.chooseA: Pick it for the quickest secure setup when you already run a backend.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when users must call the agent directly with per-user identity, or when threads need per-user access control.

compare.a: Graph compiled with your own checkpointer (InMemorySaver)
compare.difference: Agent Server injects its own persistence. Your own saver is redundant for deployment and can conflict with the platform's persistence.
compare.chooseA: Pick it only for notebooks or scripts run outside the Agent Server.
compare.chooseB: Pick it for anything served by langgraph dev, langgraph up or LangSmith Deployment.

cues.cue: hot reload, open in Studio, run locally
cues.pick: langgraph dev with langgraph.json
cues.why: It serves the graph locally, by default on port 2024, and Studio connects to it.

cues.cue: failed to load graph at startup
cues.pick: Fix the "graphs" path so it points to the compiled graph variable or a factory
cues.why: A wrong module path or an uncompiled StateGraph builder cannot be served.

cues.cue: works locally, fails on first LLM call after deploy
cues.pick: Add the model API keys as deployment environment variables
cues.why: The deployed container does not have your local secrets unless you configure them.

cues.cue: agent forgets the previous message
cues.pick: Reuse the same thread_id across runs
cues.why: Memory lives in the thread's checkpoints, and a new thread starts with no history.

cues.cue: frontend JavaScript, keep credentials safe
cues.pick: Backend proxy or custom auth
cues.why: An API key embedded in the browser can be read by anyone who opens dev tools.

cues.cue: token-by-token streaming
cues.pick: client.runs.stream with stream_mode="messages-tuple"
cues.why: It yields message chunks with metadata as the model generates them.

cues.cue: data disappears after server restart
cues.pick: Move off langgraph dev to langgraph up or LangSmith Deployment
cues.why: The dev server keeps state only in memory.

cues.cue: track cost, latency, error rate in production
cues.pick: The LangSmith tracing project and its monitoring dashboards
cues.why: Deployed runs are traced automatically, with token usage, latency and errors per run.

scenario.situation: A team deploys a create_agent chatbot to LangSmith Deployment. Their React app calls the deployment URL directly, with the LangSmith API key in a frontend env variable, and creates a thread on every send. Users say the bot forgets context, and security flags the exposed key. What is the best fix?
reasoning: Separate the two problems: the memory loss and the exposed key have different causes.

Memory loss: a new thread per message means empty state every time. Fix it by creating one thread per conversation and reusing its thread_id. Do not add InMemorySaver, because Agent Server already persists state.
Key exposure: reject any option that only hides the key in an env file. A frontend bundle is public no matter where the key is stored.
Keep options that route calls through a backend, where the SDK holds the key in x-api-key and streams to the browser, or that use custom auth in langgraph.json.
Check streaming: stream_mode="messages-tuple" keeps the token-by-token chat experience.
scenario.answer: Move the calls to a backend proxy, or add custom auth, so the LangSmith key never reaches the browser. Create one thread per conversation and reuse its thread_id for every message, streaming with messages-tuple.

memoryAids: Path to production: 'JSON → DEV → STUDIO → DEPLOY → WATCH'. Write langgraph.json, run langgraph dev, inspect in Studio, deploy, then monitor in LangSmith.
Server objects, 'A-T-R': the Assistant is the configured graph, the Thread is the conversation memory, and a Run is one execution on a thread.
'Tokens talk, updates walk': messages-tuple for live text, updates for step-by-step node progress.
cheatSheet: langgraph.json needs dependencies, graphs (id → file.py:variable) and optionally env and auth.
The graphs target must be a compiled graph or a factory, never a StateGraph builder.
Run langgraph dev locally on 127.0.0.1:2024; interactive API docs are at /docs; Studio attaches to it.
langgraph dev is in-memory, single-process and for development only. Use up or build (Docker, Postgres, Redis) or LangSmith Deployment for durability.
Never compile with your own checkpointer for the Agent Server; persistence is built in.
The default assistant_id is the graph key in langgraph.json.
Deployed endpoints need x-api-key by default; keep the key server-side.
Set model provider keys as deployment environment variables; a local .env is not a deployment secret store.
One conversation means one thread_id, reused for every message and for resuming after an interrupt.
SDK flow: get_client(url, api_key) → threads.create() → runs.stream(thread_id, assistant_id, input, stream_mode).
Use messages-tuple for chat tokens and updates for node progress.
Watch latency, token cost and error rate in the LangSmith project; tracing is automatic when deployed.
selfCheck: I can write a working langgraph.json from memory and explain each field.
I can run langgraph dev, open my agent in Studio and say why this setup is not production.
I can diagnose a 'graph failed to load' error, a missing-secret failure after deploy, and an agent that forgets context.
I can stream answers from a deployed agent through a backend with the LangGraph SDK and choose the right stream_mode.
I can explain assistants, threads and runs, and why I do not add my own checkpointer.
I can find the latency, cost and error traces for a production run in LangSmith.

objective.question: Your langgraph.json has "graphs": {"agent": "./src/agent/graph.py:builder"}, where builder is a StateGraph(State) that has nodes and edges added but has never been compiled. `langgraph dev` fails to load the graph. What is the correct fix?
options: Add "compile": true to langgraph.json so the CLI compiles the builder
Move graph.py to the project root so the path is shorter
Rename the key from "agent" to "graph" so the CLI can find the builder
Point the entry at a compiled graph variable, such as graph = builder.compile(), or at a factory function that returns a compiled graph
objective.explanation: The "graphs" value must reference a compiled graph or a factory function, never an uncompiled builder. The key name and the file location are not the problem, and there is no "compile" flag in langgraph.json.

objective.question: You run `langgraph dev` without any extra flags. Where does the local Agent Server listen, and where can you see the interactive API docs?
options: http://127.0.0.1:8123, with docs at /api
http://0.0.0.0:3000, with docs at /openapi
http://127.0.0.1:2024, with docs at /docs
http://localhost:8000, with docs at /swagger
objective.explanation: `langgraph dev` serves on http://127.0.0.1:2024 by default and exposes interactive API docs at /docs. The other ports and paths are not the CLI defaults.

objective.question: A teammate restarts `langgraph dev`, and every thread created earlier is gone. They ask whether this is a bug. What is the best explanation?
options: Threads are deleted on restart only when hot reload is turned off
`langgraph dev` keeps state in memory for development. For durable persistence, use `langgraph up` or a `langgraph build` image, which run with Postgres
Threads persist only if you compile the graph with InMemorySaver
It is a bug. `langgraph dev` always writes to a local Postgres database
objective.explanation: `langgraph dev` is a development server with in-memory state, so a restart clears it. `langgraph up` and `langgraph build` use Docker with Postgres for persistence and Redis for streaming and the task queue.

objective.question: Before deploying, you notice graph.py ends with graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()). What should you do for LangSmith Deployment?
options: Add a thread_id to the compile() call
Compile without your own checkpointer, because the Agent Server supplies persistence automatically
Replace InMemorySaver with a SQLite saver so state survives restarts
Keep it, because without it threads will not persist
objective.explanation: Agent Server handles persistence itself, so you should not compile with your own checkpointer for deployment. An in-memory or SQLite saver would bypass the managed Postgres-backed persistence. thread_id is passed at run time, not to compile().

objective.question: langgraph.json contains "graphs": {"support_bot": "./app/graph.py:graph"}, and you have not created any extra assistants. Which assistant_id should your web backend pass when it starts a run?
options: "graph"
The deployment's UUID only. Graph IDs cannot be used
"./app/graph.py:graph"
"support_bot"
objective.explanation: Unless you create extra assistants, the assistant_id you call equals the graph ID key in langgraph.json. Here that key is "support_bot". The variable name and the file path are not assistant IDs.

objective.question: You test your new LangSmith deployment with curl and get an authentication error. The request body is correct. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: An Authorization: Basic header containing your LangSmith username
Setting LANGSMITH_TRACING=true in the curl environment
The LangSmith API key in the x-api-key header
A thread_id in the query string
objective.explanation: Deployed endpoints are authenticated by default. You must send your LangSmith API key in the x-api-key header, or configure custom auth. thread_id and tracing variables have nothing to do with authentication.

objective.question: A React front end must stream chat answers from your deployed agent to public users. Which approach is secure?
options: Obfuscate the API key in the JavaScript bundle
Proxy calls through your backend, which holds the key, or add custom auth through the "auth" field in langgraph.json
Turn off authentication on the deployment so the browser needs no key
Put the LangSmith API key in a VITE_ environment variable so the browser can send x-api-key
objective.explanation: Never ship the LangSmith API key to the browser. Front-end environment variables and obfuscated bundles are readable by anyone. The supported options are a backend proxy or custom auth configured in langgraph.json.

objective.question: Product wants a ChatGPT-style UX where text appears token by token as the model generates it. Which stream_mode should the SDK call use?
options: "messages-tuple"
"debug"
"updates"
"values"
objective.explanation: Use stream_mode="messages-tuple" for token-by-token chat UX. "updates" emits node-level changes, and "values" emits full state snapshots, so neither gives smooth token streaming.

objective.question: An internal research agent runs several nodes: plan, search, summarise. Your dashboard should show a progress line such as "search finished" after each step. Which stream_mode fits best?
options: "messages-tuple"
"tokens"
"interrupts"
"updates"
objective.explanation: "updates" streams what each node returned as it completes, which gives node-level progress. "messages-tuple" is for LLM tokens, and the other two are not the modes to use for this.

objective.question: In the Agent Server model, which statement about threads and runs is correct?
options: A thread holds persisted state across many invocations, and a run is one execution of an assistant on a thread
A run can only exist without a thread, because threads are only for Studio
Threads and runs are the same object, and "run" is just the legacy name
A thread is one invocation of the graph, and a run stores conversation history across invocations
objective.explanation: A thread is the persisted conversation state, backed by checkpoints. Each run is a single execution of an assistant, either on a thread or stateless. Option A reverses the two terms, and options C and D are false.

objective.question: Locally, you run your agent with `langgraph dev` and open it in Studio, but no traces appear in your LangSmith project. After deployment to LangSmith Deployment, traces do appear. What did you most likely miss locally?
options: Compiling the graph with a LangSmith checkpointer
Switching to `langgraph up`, because `langgraph dev` cannot trace
Setting LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY, for example in the .env file referenced by langgraph.json
Adding a "tracing" key to the graphs section of langgraph.json
objective.explanation: Production tracing is automatic on LangSmith Deployment. Locally, you must set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY. There is no tracing key in graphs and no LangSmith checkpointer.

objective.question: After launch, users report that some answers take very long, and finance asks why token spend doubled. What is the most effective first step in LangSmith?
options: Read the Agent Server container logs only, because traces do not record latency or tokens
Use the tracing project's monitoring charts for latency, errors and tokens or cost, then open the slow or expensive traces and inspect the run tree to find the step responsible
Redeploy with `langgraph dev` to get hot reload in production
Re-run the offline evaluation dataset and compare scores
objective.explanation: Production traces record latency, errors and token usage per run and per step. Monitoring charts show the trends, and the run tree pinpoints the cause, such as a looping tool call. Offline evals measure quality, not live cost, and `langgraph dev` is for development only.

objective.question: A user sends a second chat message while the agent is still answering the first. Product wants the first run stopped and fully discarded, as if it never happened, before the new message is processed. Which multitask_strategy should the web backend pass when it starts the new run?

code.code:
await client.runs.stream(
    thread_id,
    "agent",
    input={"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": new_text}]},
    stream_mode="messages-tuple",
    multitask_strategy=???,
)

options: "rollback"
"enqueue"
"interrupt"
"reject"
objective.explanation: "rollback" cancels the in-flight run and deletes it, including its progress, before starting the new run. "interrupt" also stops the first run but keeps its partial progress on the thread. "reject" refuses the new run, and "enqueue" queues it until the first run finishes.

objective.question: A tool inside your agent downloads and parses a large PDF. You want the web UI to show messages such as "Parsed page 3 of 40" while the tool runs. Which combination achieves this?
options: Return the progress text from the tool and stream with stream_mode="updates"
Use print() inside the tool and read the server logs from the browser
Call the tool's writer and stream with stream_mode="values"
Call the tool's writer and stream with stream_mode="custom"
objective.explanation: Data sent through get_stream_writer() is emitted on the "custom" stream mode, so the client must request stream_mode="custom" (it can be combined with other modes). "values" and "updates" carry graph state, not writer output, and print() never reaches the client.

objective.question: A company runs a one-off email classification call on its deployed graph for each incoming email. It does not need conversation history and wants no threads left behind. What is the simplest correct approach with the LangGraph SDK?
options: Start a stateless run by passing None as the thread_id
Compile the graph with checkpointer=None in langgraph.json
Reuse one shared thread_id for all emails
Create a new thread per email, then delete it after the run
objective.explanation: Passing None as the thread_id (for example client.runs.wait(None, "agent", input=...)) creates a stateless run with no stored thread. Creating and deleting threads adds needless calls. A shared thread mixes state across emails. langgraph.json has no per-graph compile setting like this.

objective.question: One deployed graph, graph_id "support_bot", must serve two brands. Each brand needs a different system prompt and model. The code already reads both values from runtime configuration. What is the recommended way to do this without a redeploy?
options: Add a second entry with the same file path to "graphs" in langgraph.json
Create two assistants from graph_id "support_bot" with different configuration, and pass each assistant_id from the brand's backend
Pass the system prompt inside every user message
Deploy the same repository twice, once per brand
objective.explanation: Assistants are configured instances of a graph. client.assistants.create(graph_id="support_bot", ...) with brand-specific settings lets each backend choose an assistant_id, with no new deployment. Separate deployments or duplicate graph entries add cost and maintenance, and prompts in user messages are fragile and unsafe.

objective.question: A nightly job sends 500 long research tasks to your deployed agent. Each task can take several minutes. The calling script should not hold an HTTP connection open for each task, and it needs to be told when each task finishes. Which design fits best?
options: client.runs.wait for each task, with a long client timeout
client.runs.create to start background runs with a webhook URL, so the server calls back on completion
Run the 500 tasks in a single run with a huge input list
client.runs.stream for each task, keeping all streams open
objective.explanation: runs.create starts a background run and returns at once. A webhook (or a later runs.join) delivers the result without holding a connection for each task. Streaming or waiting ties up connections for minutes, and one giant run removes per-task isolation and retries.

objective.question: Your team wants every production trace sampled at 10% and scored automatically for helpfulness by an LLM judge. Production traffic has no reference answers. What should you set up in LangSmith?
options: An online evaluator (LLM-as-judge) on the tracing project with a 10% sampling rate
A HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on every tool call
An alert on the latency P99 metric
A dataset of production inputs and a nightly evaluate() call with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT
objective.explanation: Online evaluators run on live traces in a tracing project. They support sampling and need no reference outputs, so they suit a reference-free criterion like helpfulness. CORRECTNESS_PROMPT expects reference answers and offline datasets. Latency alerts do not score quality, and HITL middleware pauses the agent rather than evaluating it.

objective.question: What does the "dependencies" field in this langgraph.json tell the LangGraph CLI and the Agent Server?
options: Load every .py file in the current folder as a separate graph
Share dependencies with other deployments in the same workspace
Copy the .env file into the container as a dependency
Install the local package in the project root, using its pyproject.toml or requirements file, when building the server image
objective.explanation: "dependencies" lists packages or local paths to install. "." means install the project in the config's directory using its dependency file. Graphs are registered only in "graphs", "env" is a separate field, and dependencies are not shared across deployments.

objective.question: Which order of steps takes a local agent to a public URL that streams answers?
options: Create a LangSmith Deployment → write langgraph.json → push the repo to GitHub → run `langgraph dev` → add secrets after the first failed call
Write langgraph.json → create the deployment → run `langgraph dev` in production mode → embed the LangSmith API key in the front end to test streaming
Push the repo to GitHub → run `langgraph dev` against the deployment URL → write langgraph.json → open Studio

Install langgraph-cli[inmem] → write langgraph.json → run `langgraph dev` and test in Studio → push the repo to GitHub → create a LangSmith Deployment and add secrets as environment variables → call the deployment URL with the SDK using streaming
objective.explanation: You validate locally with the CLI and Studio first, then deploy from the repo with secrets configured, then test streaming against the public URL. The other orders deploy untested code, treat `langgraph dev` as production, or leak the API key.

objective.question: `langgraph dev` fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'agent'. The project has a pyproject.toml that defines the agent package. What is the correct fix?
options: Add "." to "dependencies" so the project and its package are installed into the server environment
Change the graph path to "agent.graph:graph" and keep dependencies empty
Copy the tools code into graph.py so no imports are needed
Set PYTHONPATH=src in the .env file
objective.explanation: "dependencies": ["."] tells the CLI to install your local project, so `agent` becomes importable both locally and in the deployment image. PYTHONPATH hacks and copying code are fragile workarounds, and changing the path syntax does not install the package.

objective.question: This backend loop streams from a deployed agent with stream_mode="messages-tuple". No text is ever printed, but the run succeeds. What is the cause?

code.code:
async for chunk in client.runs.stream(
    thread_id, "agent",
    input={"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}]},
    stream_mode="messages-tuple",
):
    if chunk.event == "values":
        print(chunk.data["messages"][-1]["content"])

options: With messages-tuple the events are named "messages", and chunk.data is a (message_chunk, metadata) pair, so the "values" branch never runs
The SDK buffers messages-tuple output until the run ends
The assistant must be created with streaming=True first
messages-tuple only works on threadless runs
objective.explanation: Each stream mode emits its own event type. messages-tuple produces "messages" events that carry a message chunk plus metadata, so you must check for that event and read the chunk's content. No assistant flag or thread type is involved.

objective.question: Users say the deployed chatbot forgets their name on the next message. Your backend handler looks like this. What is the fix?

code.code:
@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    thread = await client.threads.create()
    return StreamingResponse(
        relay(client.runs.stream(
            thread["thread_id"], "agent",
            input={"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": req.text}]},
            stream_mode="messages-tuple")),
        media_type="text/event-stream")

options: Create the thread once per conversation, store its thread_id (for example against the user's session), and reuse it on every message
Send the full chat history in input on every request and keep creating new threads
Switch to stream_mode="values" so state is returned and kept
Compile the graph with InMemorySaver so the server remembers messages
objective.explanation: Memory on the Agent Server lives in the thread's checkpoints, so a new thread per message means an empty history every time. Adding InMemorySaver conflicts with platform persistence, and resending history wastes tokens and bypasses the thread model.

objective.question: `langgraph dev` is running, but Studio opened in Safari cannot connect to the local server at 127.0.0.1:2024. Chrome works. What is the recommended fix?
options: Deploy to LangSmith Deployment, because Studio only works with deployed agents
Disable LangSmith tracing so Studio stops calling the server
Change the port to 80 in langgraph.json
Run `langgraph dev --tunnel` so Studio connects through a secure tunnel URL instead of localhost
objective.explanation: Safari blocks plain-HTTP connections to localhost from the Studio web page, and the docs recommend the --tunnel flag for this case. Studio does work with local servers, and changing the port or tracing settings does not solve the browser restriction.

objective.question: Locally the agent works. Your .env holds OPENAI_API_KEY and is listed in .gitignore. langgraph.json has "env": ".env". After deploying from GitHub, the first model call fails with an authentication error. What should you do?
options: Hard-code the key in graph.py behind an if-statement for production
Add OPENAI_API_KEY as an environment variable or secret in the deployment's settings, then redeploy or restart the revision
Pass the OpenAI key in the x-api-key header from the client
Remove .env from .gitignore and commit it so the deployment can read it
objective.explanation: The ignored .env never reaches the deployment, so the key must be set in the deployment configuration. Committing or hard-coding secrets leaks them, and x-api-key authenticates to LangSmith, not to the model provider.

objective.question: Your web backend resumes a paused HumanInTheLoopMiddleware approval like this. The resume has no effect, and the original run stays paused. What is the mistake?

code.code:
# user clicked Approve in the UI
thread = await client.threads.create()
result = await client.runs.wait(
    thread["thread_id"], "agent",
    command={"resume": decision},
)

options: The resume must target the same thread_id as the interrupted run. A fresh thread has no pending interrupt
command must be passed as input={"resume": decision}
Interrupts expire as soon as the HTTP connection closes, so the user must start over
runs.wait cannot send commands; only runs.create can
objective.explanation: An interrupt is saved in the thread's checkpoint, so Command(resume) only works on that same thread. The command parameter is correct, and interrupts persist on the server until they are resumed.

objective.question: You registered this auth module in langgraph.json. Logins work, but any logged-in user can list and read other users' threads. What is missing?
options: An @auth.on authorization handler that stamps the owner into resource metadata on create and returns a filter such as {"owner": ctx.user.identity}
Create one assistant per user so their threads are separate
Set multitask_strategy="reject" on every run
The handler must return the LangSmith API key so the server can scope data
objective.explanation: @auth.authenticate only proves who the user is. Authorization handlers registered with @auth.on decide what that user can access, by tagging metadata and filtering reads. Assistants and multitask strategies do not restrict thread access.

objective.question: The on-call engineer must be notified when the production agent's error rate goes above a threshold over a short window, without anyone watching a dashboard. What should you set up?
options: A nightly evaluate() experiment on a curated dataset
An alert rule on the production tracing project in LangSmith, based on error rate or count, routed to a notification channel
A Studio session left open on the deployment
An online LLM-as-judge evaluator on 10% of traces
objective.explanation: LangSmith alerts watch project metrics such as errors, latency and feedback, and notify a channel when a threshold is crossed. Online evaluators score quality, offline experiments test before release, and Studio is an interactive debugger rather than a monitor.

objective.question: A trace shows one conversation in which the agent called the model 60 times in a loop between two tools, and it burned a large share of the day's budget. What is the most direct guardrail?
options: Switch the client to stream_mode="updates"
Add a model call limit middleware, and a tool call limit where needed, so the run stops after a set number of calls
Add PIIMiddleware to redact the tool inputs
Add SummarizationMiddleware with a lower token trigger
objective.explanation: Call limit middleware caps model or tool calls per run or thread, which directly stops runaway loops. Summarization only shrinks the context of each call, PII redaction is about privacy, and stream mode changes what the client sees, not what the agent spends.

objective.question: You need a /stripe-webhook POST endpoint served by the same Agent Server as your graph. Which langgraph.json change is correct?
options: Add "routes": ["/stripe-webhook"]
Add the route to "auth": {"path": ...}
Add "webhooks": {"stripe": "./src/webapp.py:handler"}
Add "http": {"app": "./src/webapp.py:app"}, pointing at a FastAPI or Starlette app that defines the route
objective.explanation: The "http" field with an "app" path mounts your own ASGI app alongside the built-in Agent Server routes. The "routes" and "webhooks" keys do not exist in langgraph.json, and "auth" is only for authentication and authorization handlers.

objective.question: Spot the mistake in this langgraph.json graph entry.
options: The file path and the variable name must be separated by a colon: "./src/agent/graph.py:graph"
Paths must be absolute
"dependencies" must list langgraph explicitly
The graph id must be "graph", not "agent"
objective.explanation: The format is path/to/file.py:variable, so a dot instead of the colon breaks graph loading. The graph id can be any name, relative paths are normal, and "." installs the project's declared dependencies.

objective.question: To prove the checkpoint "a public URL streams answers", which test is the strongest evidence?
options: Call POST /runs/wait on the deployment URL and check that the final answer is correct
POST to the deployment URL's /threads/{thread_id}/runs/stream with the x-api-key header and stream_mode "messages-tuple", and see SSE events arrive incrementally before the run ends
Check that the deployment shows a green status in LangSmith
Open the agent in Studio using `langgraph dev` and watch the answer appear
objective.explanation: Only a request to the deployed URL's streaming endpoint shows that tokens arrive incrementally from the public deployment. Studio on `langgraph dev` is local, /runs/wait returns only the final result, and a healthy status does not prove streaming works.

subjective.question: Walk me through a minimal langgraph.json and what each field does.
subjective.answer: A minimal file is {"dependencies": ["."], "graphs": {"agent": "./src/agent/graph.py:graph"}, "env": ".env"}. The "dependencies" field tells the CLI and the Agent Server what to install. "." means install the current project from its pyproject.toml or requirements. The "graphs" field maps a graph ID to a path in the form file:variable. That variable must be a compiled graph, such as the result of create_agent or StateGraph.compile(), or a factory function. The graph ID, here "agent", becomes the default assistant_id. The "env" field points to an environment file holding the model keys and the LANGSMITH_* variables for local runs. You can also add an "auth" field to plug in custom authentication. The same file drives `langgraph dev`, `langgraph up`, `langgraph build` and LangSmith Deployment, so it is the single contract between your code and the server.
keyPoints: dependencies tells the CLI and server what to install; "." installs the current project
graphs maps an ID to file:variable, which must be a compiled graph or a factory
The graph ID becomes the default assistant_id
env points to the environment file; auth adds custom authentication
One file serves the CLI, Docker builds and deployment

subjective.question: Why must the "graphs" entry point to a compiled graph or a factory function, and when would you use a factory?
subjective.answer: The Agent Server needs a runnable graph it can invoke, stream and checkpoint. A StateGraph builder is only a definition. It cannot run until compile() is called, so pointing at the builder fails to load. create_agent already returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so you can export it directly. A factory function is useful when the graph depends on something known only at run time, for example choosing a model, a set of tools or a system prompt from the assistant's configuration. The server calls the factory to get a compiled graph. In both cases, do not attach your own checkpointer, because the server injects persistence. In an interview I would add that this is the most common load error. The traceback usually says the object is not a graph, and the fix is a one-line compile().
keyPoints: A builder is only a definition; the server needs something it can execute
create_agent already returns a compiled graph
A factory builds the graph from run-time configuration
Do not attach your own checkpointer in either case

subjective.question: Compare `langgraph dev` with `langgraph up` and `langgraph build`. When do you use each?
subjective.answer: `langgraph dev` is the fast inner loop. It runs an Agent Server in-process on http://127.0.0.1:2024 with no Docker. It keeps state in memory, hot-reloads when code changes, and exposes API docs at /docs. It also lets LangSmith Studio connect to your local agent. Because state lives in memory, a restart wipes threads, so it is for development only. `langgraph up` runs the server in Docker with Postgres for persistence and Redis for streaming and the task queue. That makes it close to production, which is good for testing durability, concurrency and restarts. `langgraph build` produces a Docker image that you can push and run on your own infrastructure. My usual flow is: iterate with dev and Studio, verify with up, and then ship through LangSmith Deployment or a built image.
keyPoints: dev runs without Docker, keeps state in memory, hot-reloads and serves on port 2024
dev supports Studio and is for development only
up runs Docker with Postgres for persistence and Redis for streaming and the queue
build produces a deployable Docker image

subjective.question: How do you open a local agent in LangSmith Studio, and what do you use Studio for?
subjective.answer: First I make sure langgraph.json points at my compiled graph and that the .env file has my model keys plus LANGSMITH_API_KEY. Then I run `langgraph dev` in the project folder. It starts the local Agent Server on 127.0.0.1:2024 and prints a Studio link, which opens Studio connected to that local server. In Studio I can see the graph's nodes and edges, send inputs, and watch each step stream. I can also inspect state at every checkpoint, fork a thread from an earlier state, and test interrupts by resuming with a value. Because dev hot-reloads, I can edit a prompt or a tool, rerun the same thread and compare results. Traces go to LangSmith, so I can debug in Studio and then open the full trace for token counts and latency.
keyPoints: Run `langgraph dev` with a valid langgraph.json and .env
Studio connects to the local server on port 2024
Use it to visualise the graph, inspect and fork state, and test interrupts
Hot reload makes prompt and tool iteration fast

subjective.question: A junior developer compiled the graph with InMemorySaver and deployed it. Explain what is wrong and how persistence works on the Agent Server.
subjective.answer: On the Agent Server, persistence is a platform feature. The server manages checkpoints for every thread in its own durable storage, which is Postgres in the Docker and deployed setups. If you compile with your own checkpointer, you either conflict with or bypass that system. InMemorySaver in particular lives in one process's memory. State would vanish on restart and would not be shared across replicas, so multi-turn conversations and human-in-the-loop resumes would break unpredictably. The fix is to compile without a checkpointer, or export the create_agent result without one, and let the server inject persistence. Threads are then created through the API, and each run on a thread_id resumes from the latest checkpoint. Locally, InMemorySaver is still fine for plain Python scripts and notebooks. It just should not be in the graph you deploy.
keyPoints: The Agent Server supplies persistence automatically
A custom checkpointer conflicts with or bypasses managed storage
InMemorySaver loses state on restart and is not shared across replicas
Compile without a checkpointer and use threads through the API

subjective.question: Explain assistants, threads and runs on the Agent Server, with an example for a support chatbot.
subjective.answer: An assistant is a graph plus its configuration. By default, each graph ID in langgraph.json is an assistant, so "support" is callable as assistant_id "support". You can create extra assistants from the same graph with different configuration, for example a Hindi-language support assistant. A thread is a persisted conversation. It stores the graph's state through checkpoints, so one customer's chat becomes one thread. A run is a single execution of an assistant, usually on a thread. When the customer sends a new message, my backend starts a run on their thread_id. The graph loads the latest state, processes the message and saves a new checkpoint. Runs can be streamed, waited on, or queued in the background. With this separation, one deployed graph can serve many configurations and many users without mixing their state.
keyPoints: An assistant is a graph plus configuration; the default ID equals the graph key
Extra assistants can reuse one graph with different settings
A thread is persisted state across turns
A run is one execution on a thread, which can be streamed or run in the background

subjective.question: Design how a public web app streams answers from your deployed agent. Cover the request path and the SDK calls.
subjective.answer: The browser never talks to the deployment directly, because that would expose the API key. The browser calls my backend, for example a FastAPI endpoint. The backend creates a client with the LangGraph SDK: get_client(url=DEPLOYMENT_URL, api_key=LANGSMITH_API_KEY), where the key comes from a server-side secret. On a user's first message, the backend calls client.threads.create() and stores the thread_id against the user's session. For each message, it calls client.runs.stream(thread_id, "agent", input={"messages": [...]}, stream_mode="messages-tuple"). It then relays each chunk to the browser over Server-Sent Events or a streaming HTTP response, and the UI appends tokens as they arrive. The backend should also handle disconnects and errors, and enforce my own user authentication. The alternative is custom auth configured in langgraph.json, which lets the front end call the deployment with user tokens instead.
keyPoints: Never put the LangSmith key in the browser; proxy through a backend or use custom auth
Create one thread per conversation and store its thread_id
Call runs.stream with the assistant_id and stream_mode messages-tuple
Relay chunks to the browser through SSE or a streaming response

subjective.question: When would you choose stream_mode="messages-tuple" versus "updates"? Can you use both?
subjective.answer: "messages-tuple" streams LLM output token by token, together with metadata such as which node produced it. That is what you want for a chat interface where text should appear as it is generated. The metadata lets the UI filter out tokens from internal nodes, such as a planner, that users should not see. "updates" streams the output of each node as it finishes, for example "the search node returned five documents". That suits progress indicators, step logs or agent dashboards where node-level granularity matters more than individual tokens. You can request several modes in one call by passing a list, then branch on the event type in your handler. That way the UI can show live tokens and a step tracker at once. In practice, chat products lean on messages-tuple, and workflow or back-office tools lean on updates.
keyPoints: messages-tuple streams tokens plus metadata for chat UX
Metadata lets the UI filter tokens from internal nodes
updates streams per-node outputs for progress views
A list of modes can be combined in one stream

subjective.question: How do you secure a deployed agent endpoint?
subjective.answer: By default, LangSmith Deployment endpoints require authentication. Every call must carry a LangSmith API key in the x-api-key header. That key is effectively an admin credential, so it belongs only on servers. I keep it in a secret manager or in the deployment environment and never in front-end code or in git. For a public app, I have two options. The first is a backend proxy that authenticates my users with my own system and then calls the agent with the key. The second is custom auth, registered through the "auth" field in langgraph.json. With custom auth, the server validates user tokens itself, and I can scope resources so each user sees only their own threads. I would also rotate keys, use separate keys per environment, and watch the error rate for spikes in rejected requests.
keyPoints: Endpoints are authenticated by default with x-api-key
The LangSmith key must never reach the browser
Use a backend proxy or custom auth through the "auth" field
Custom auth can scope threads per user; rotate and separate keys per environment

subjective.question: Your agent is in production. How do you monitor cost, latency and errors, and what would you act on?
subjective.answer: On LangSmith Deployment, tracing is automatic, so every run lands in a tracing project with its full run tree, latency, token counts, cost estimates and any errors. I start with the project's monitoring charts for trace volume, p50 and p99 latency, error rate, and token usage or cost over time. I set alerts on error rate and latency thresholds. When a metric moves, I filter traces, for example errored runs or runs above a latency cutoff, and open the run tree. That shows whether the problem is a slow tool, a retry storm or a model looping through tool calls. For cost, I look for long contexts and add SummarizationMiddleware or model call limits, or move simple steps to a cheaper model. Tagging runs with metadata such as user tier or release version lets me compare versions. I would also add online evaluators for quality.
keyPoints: Tracing is automatic on LangSmith Deployment
Track volume, p50 and p99 latency, error rate and tokens or cost
Set alerts, then drill into filtered traces and run trees
Cut cost with summarisation, call limits or cheaper models; tag runs by version

subjective.question: An agent works with `langgraph dev` but fails after deployment. How do you debug it?
subjective.answer: I work through the usual suspects in order. First, dependencies: "dependencies" in langgraph.json must cover everything. A package installed only in my local virtual environment, but missing from pyproject.toml or requirements, will fail in the build. Second, environment variables: the .env file is for local runs, so model keys and other secrets must be configured in the deployment's environment settings. Third, the graph path: the file:variable must resolve inside the built project, and it must point to a compiled graph or a factory. Fourth, persistence: remove any checkpointer I compiled in, because the server provides one. Fifth, the client: is it sending x-api-key, and is the assistant_id equal to the graph key? Then I read the deployment's build and server logs and open the failing trace in LangSmith to see which node broke. Reproducing with `langgraph up` locally is closest to production.
keyPoints: Check that dependencies are complete in langgraph.json and the project files
Configure secrets in the deployment environment, not only in .env
Verify the graph path points to a compiled graph and remove custom checkpointers
Check x-api-key and assistant_id, then use logs, traces and `langgraph up` to reproduce

subjective.question: Your deployed agent uses HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on send_email. How does a web app handle the pause and resume through the API?
subjective.answer: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware calls interrupt when the agent tries to call send_email. The run pauses, and the thread's state is saved by the Agent Server's persistence, so I do not need my own checkpointer. While streaming, my backend sees the interrupt event with its payload, such as the proposed email and the allowed decisions: approve, edit or reject. The backend forwards that to the UI as an approval card. When the user decides, the backend starts a new run on the same thread_id with a resume command. In the Python SDK, that means passing command={"resume": ...} with the decision to client.runs.stream. The interrupted node re-runs from its start, so any side effects before the interrupt should be idempotent. Using a different thread_id would start a fresh conversation, and the pending action would be lost.
keyPoints: The interrupt pauses the run and the server persists the thread state
The interrupt payload is surfaced in the stream and shown to the user
Resume with a resume command on the same thread_id
The node re-runs from its start, so pre-interrupt side effects must be idempotent

subjective.question: Explain the double-texting strategies on the Agent Server (reject, interrupt, rollback, enqueue). Which would you choose for a customer chat app, and why?
subjective.answer: Double texting means a new run arrives on a thread while another run is still active. The multitask_strategy tells the server what to do. "reject" refuses the new run and keeps the first one. "enqueue" queues the new run until the current one finishes. "interrupt" stops the current run but keeps its partial progress on the thread, then starts the new run. "rollback" stops the current run and deletes it with its progress, then starts the new run. For a customer chat app where users often send a quick correction such as "sorry, I meant order 42", I would use "interrupt" or "rollback". Rollback gives a clean history if partial answers would confuse the model. Interrupt keeps context the user may already have seen. For tasks that must all complete, like form submissions, I would choose "enqueue". I set the strategy per call in runs.create or runs.stream and test it in Studio before launch.
keyPoints: Double texting is a new run on a busy thread
Clear definition of all four strategies
Difference between interrupt (keeps progress) and rollback (deletes it)
Choice justified by the UX, with enqueue for must-complete tasks

subjective.question: What does this auth module do once it is registered in langgraph.json? How does it isolate users' threads?
subjective.answer: This is custom authentication and authorisation for the Agent Server. You register it in langgraph.json with an "auth" entry pointing to the object, for example {"path": "./src/auth.py:auth"}. The @auth.authenticate handler runs on every request. It verifies the bearer token, here a JWT from our identity provider, and returns the user's identity. If the token is invalid, it raises an error and the request is rejected. The @auth.on handler is a global authorisation handler for resources such as threads, runs and assistants. When a resource is created, it stamps owner=user_id into the metadata. The filter it returns is applied to reads, searches and updates. As a result, user A can never list or stream user B's threads, even with a valid thread_id. In production, I add narrower handlers for specific resources and actions where needed. I also test the setup with two tokens to prove isolation works.
keyPoints: Registered via the "auth" field in langgraph.json
authenticate verifies the token and returns an identity
@auth.on adds owner metadata on create
Returned filters restrict access to the owner's resources
Test isolation with two different users

subjective.question: A client needs your deployed agent to process long reports in the background and also run a summary every morning. How would you design this with the Agent Server APIs?
subjective.answer: I would not use streaming for these jobs. For on-demand reports, the backend calls client.runs.create on a thread, or on None for a stateless run, with the assistant_id and input. This starts a background run and returns a run ID immediately. To get the result, I pass a webhook URL so the server notifies our service when the run completes. Alternatively, a worker can call client.runs.join to wait for the result, or poll the run status. Because the server handles persistence, the state is safe even if our worker restarts. For the morning summary, I would use a cron job on the Agent Server. It creates runs on a schedule for a given assistant and input, so I don't need a separate scheduler. In LangSmith, I would tag these runs with metadata such as job="daily_summary". That lets me filter their traces and set alerts on failures and latency separately from chat traffic.
keyPoints: runs.create for background runs that return at once
Webhook or runs.join or polling to collect results
Server-side persistence survives worker restarts
Cron jobs for scheduled runs
Tag runs with metadata for monitoring

subjective.question: Marketing wants to change the agent's system prompt and model weekly without involving engineering redeploys. How do assistants and their versions support this safely?
subjective.answer: I write the graph so the system prompt and model name come from runtime configuration, not hard-coded constants. Each deployed graph gets a default assistant. I then create a named assistant, for example "marketing_bot", with client.assistants.create and set the prompt and model there. When marketing wants a change, we update that assistant. Each update creates a new assistant version, and the deployment itself does not change. The web backend always calls the same assistant_id, so the change goes live with no code release. If a new prompt performs badly, we roll back by setting the assistant to an earlier version. Before switching, I run the new configuration against a LangSmith dataset with evaluate() and compare experiments with the current version. Code changes, such as new tools or new nodes, still need a real deployment revision. Assistants only change configuration.
keyPoints: Read prompt and model from configuration in the graph
Create or update a named assistant from the graph_id
Updates create versions; roll back to an earlier version
Backend keeps the same assistant_id
Evaluate before switching; code changes still need redeploys

subjective.question: Explain how environment variables and secrets should be handled for this agent, both locally with `langgraph dev` and on LangSmith Deployment.
subjective.answer: Locally, the "env" field tells the CLI to load variables from the .env file. That file holds keys such as OPENAI_API_KEY, LANGSMITH_API_KEY and LANGSMITH_TRACING=true. It must be in .gitignore and never committed, so I keep a .env.example with blank values for teammates. "python_version" pins the runtime for the built image, and "dependencies" makes sure the project's packages are installed. For LangSmith Deployment, I do not rely on the committed repo to carry secrets. I enter the model provider keys and other secrets as environment variables or secrets in the deployment's settings, and I use separate values for dev and prod deployments. Code reads them with os.environ, so the same code works in both places. A common failure is a key that exists locally but was never added to the deployment. The deployment logs show this quickly. I also rotate keys if they ever appear in a trace or a log.
keyPoints: "env" loads .env for local runs; keep it out of git
Secrets are set in the deployment settings, not in the repo
Separate values for dev and prod deployments
python_version and dependencies control the build
A missing secret is a common post-deploy failure; check the logs

subjective.question: How would you turn production traffic into a regression test suite for your deployed agent using LangSmith?
subjective.answer: First, I collect signal. The web app sends user feedback, such as thumbs up or down, to LangSmith, attached to the run ID. Online evaluators also score a sample of traces. Next, I set up automation rules on the tracing project. For example, runs with negative feedback or low judge scores go to an annotation queue, and good examples go straight into a dataset. In the queue, reviewers correct the output, and the corrected answer becomes the reference for that example. Over time, the dataset covers real failure cases, not just made-up ones. Before every release, CI calls evaluate() with the new agent against this dataset. Evaluators include create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT and simple checks such as tool-call accuracy. I compare the new experiment with the last production baseline in LangSmith. If scores drop on key slices, the release is blocked. This closes the loop: monitor, curate, evaluate, deploy.
keyPoints: Capture user feedback and online evaluator scores on traces
Rules route bad runs to annotation queues and datasets
Human-corrected outputs become reference answers
evaluate() in CI against the curated dataset
Compare experiments with the baseline and gate the release

subjective.question: You have a working production deployment. Describe a safe process for shipping a new version of the agent code.
subjective.answer: I keep two deployments: a development deployment for testing and a production deployment for users. Each has its own secrets and tracing project. The code lives in Git. A merge to the main branch, or a manual action, creates a new revision on the development deployment. I then test it in Studio against that deployment and run a smoke test. The smoke test uses the SDK to create a thread, stream with messages-tuple and check that the answer arrives. I also run evaluate() on the regression dataset and compare the results with production's baseline experiment. If quality, latency and cost per run are acceptable, I deploy the same commit to production. After the release, I watch the LangSmith monitoring charts for error rate, P50 and P99 latency, and token cost for the first hours, with alerts enabled. If something breaks, I roll back to the previous revision. I avoid changing graph state schemas in ways that break existing threads. If I must change them, I make the changes backward compatible.
keyPoints: Separate dev and prod deployments with their own secrets and projects
New revision tested in Studio plus an SDK streaming smoke test
evaluate() gate against a baseline experiment
Post-release monitoring with alerts, and rollback to the previous revision
Keep state changes backward compatible for existing threads

subjective.question: Case study: a coaching institute wants a public FAQ chatbot on its website. Requirements: answers stream token by token, each student keeps their conversation across visits, no secret reaches the browser, and the team can see cost per day and get alerts on errors. Design the full solution.
subjective.answer: I build the agent with create_agent and compile it without a checkpointer. I add langgraph.json with dependencies ["."] and a graphs entry pointing at the compiled graph, then test it with `langgraph dev` and Studio. I deploy from GitHub to LangSmith Deployment and put the model key in the deployment's environment variables. The browser talks only to our backend, which checks the student's session. The backend stores one thread_id per student conversation in our database and reuses it, so memory persists across visits.
