revision.examFocus: This step maps to the capstone and interview stage of the path. LangChain Academy courses are free and self-paced with no proctored exam, so the real test is a technical interview or demo. In that setting you are asked to explain why your agent pauses, resumes, traces and scores the way it does. Expect questions on checkpointer and thread_id behaviour, interrupt and resume semantics, evaluation design, and why you chose subagents over langgraph-supervisor.

compare.b: invoke with a new user message
compare.difference: Command(resume=...) feeds the human decision into the paused node and continues the saved run. A new message starts a fresh turn and leaves the pending interrupt unanswered.
compare.chooseA: Pick this when the graph reports an interrupt and you need to pass approve, edit or reject back to it.
compare.chooseB: Pick this only when there is no pending interrupt and the user is asking something new.

compare.b: interrupt() inside a custom StateGraph node
compare.difference: The middleware gates specific tool calls declaratively through interrupt_on. A raw interrupt() lets you pause anywhere, but you own the node design and must keep it idempotent.
compare.chooseA: Pick this when approval is needed before a named tool runs, such as send_email.
compare.chooseB: Pick this when the pause point is custom logic outside a tool call, inside your own graph.

compare.difference: Tracing records what happened in individual runs. evaluate() runs a target over a dataset with evaluators and gives a comparable experiment with scores.
compare.chooseA: Pick tracing to debug one failing run or to inspect tool calls and latency.
compare.chooseB: Pick evaluate() to prove quality with numbers or to compare two prompt or model versions.

compare.a: Subagents pattern (main create_agent with tools wrapping workers)
compare.difference: The subagents pattern is the current recommended approach. langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained.
compare.chooseA: Pick this for any new multi-agent design, with a checkpointer only on the outer agent.
compare.chooseB: Pick it only when explaining legacy code you are migrating away from.

compare.difference: create_agent is the general agent builder; you add the middleware you need. create_deep_agent pre-assembles filesystem, summarization, subagents and prompt caching for long-running tasks.
compare.chooseA: Pick this for a focused capstone with RAG, one approval-gated tool and a clear eval set.
compare.chooseB: Pick this for long, multi-stage research or coding tasks that need planning and file workspaces.

cues.cue: agent forgets the conversation / resume starts over
cues.pick: Missing or changed thread_id in config
cues.why: The checkpointer keys saved state by thread_id, so no id or a new id means no state to load.

cues.cue: approval email sent twice / duplicate DB row after resume
cues.pick: Move side effects after interrupt() or into a separate node
cues.why: The interrupted node re-runs from its start on resume, so earlier work repeats.

cues.cue: require a human to approve before a tool runs
cues.pick: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with interrupt_on and allowed_decisions
cues.why: It gates named tool calls without hand-writing graph nodes.

cues.cue: prove the agent answers correctly with scores
cues.pick: LangSmith dataset + evaluate() + openevals create_llm_as_judge(CORRECTNESS_PROMPT)
cues.why: This produces an experiment with per-example and aggregate scores you can link.

cues.cue: visually debug a local agent step by step
cues.pick: langgraph dev with langgraph.json, then open LangSmith Studio
cues.why: Studio connects to the locally served graph for inspection and interaction.

cues.cue: no traces appear in LangSmith
cues.pick: Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY in the environment
cues.why: Tracing is off unless both are present.

cues.cue: inspect or time-travel to an earlier step
cues.pick: graph.get_state_history(config)
cues.why: It lists saved checkpoints for the thread, newest first.

cues.cue: multi-agent state is duplicated or conflicting
cues.pick: Checkpointer only on the outermost graph
cues.why: Inner subagents should not persist separately; the parent owns persistence.

scenario.situation: Your capstone is a support agent built with create_agent. It has a retrieval tool over product docs and a send_email tool gated by HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, and it is compiled with InMemorySaver. In a demo, the agent pauses for email approval. Your frontend then sends invoke({'messages': [...'approve'...]}) with a freshly generated thread_id, and the email is never sent. What is the correct fix?
reasoning: The agent did pause, so the middleware and the checkpointer are wired correctly. Rule out reconfiguring interrupt_on.
A fresh thread_id points to an empty checkpoint, so the paused run cannot be found.
Sending 'approve' as a new user message starts a new turn. It does not answer the pending interrupt.
Swapping InMemorySaver for a durable store helps across restarts, but it does not fix a wrong id or the wrong resume call.
scenario.answer: Reuse the original thread_id and resume with Command(resume=...), passing the approve decision in the format the middleware expects. This continues the saved run at the paused tool call, so send_email executes.

memoryAids: T-I-R: Thread id always, Interrupt pauses, Resume with Command on the same thread.
Side effects AFTER the pause: 'Ask first, act after', because the node replays from the top.
README = D-E-D: Diagram, Evaluation numbers (dataset size, evaluator names, scores, experiment link), Demo link.
cheatSheet: Academy courses are free and self-paced. In this step you finish LangGraph and LangSmith; interviews test your capstone, not a certificate score.
Langflow has no official certification. A published flow built from the official docs and tutorials is your evidence.
create_agent from langchain.agents returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so stream, state history and Studio all work on it.
Always pass config={'configurable': {'thread_id': ...}} when a checkpointer is used.
Resume = Command(resume=value) + same thread_id. A new message or a new id does not resume.
Keep code before interrupt() pure and idempotent, because the node restarts on resume.
Drive the graph with stream_events(..., version='v3') to detect interrupts cleanly in a UI.
Tracing: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true + LANGSMITH_API_KEY. Studio: langgraph dev + langgraph.json.
evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]) creates a named experiment. Link it in your README.
Keep eval examples on retrieval Q&A, or auto-handle approvals inside the target function.
Multi-agent: use the subagents pattern, not langgraph-supervisor, with one checkpointer at the top.
Treat RAG as a tool the agent chooses to call, so its use is visible in traces and testable in evals.
selfCheck: I can demo my capstone live: ask a question, watch retrieval in the trace, approve an email, and show it resume on the same thread.
I can explain why a missing thread_id or a wrong resume call breaks human approval, and fix it in code.
I can show a LangSmith experiment with dataset size, evaluator names and scores, and explain one failing example.
I can justify the subagents pattern over langgraph-supervisor and say where the checkpointer goes.
I can run langgraph dev with langgraph.json and inspect my agent in LangSmith Studio.
I have both Academy courses (LangGraph and LangSmith) completed and a README with diagram, numbers and demo link.

objective.question: You are starting your capstone agent with LangChain v1. Which import and return type are correct for create_agent?
options: from langchain.agents import create_agent; it returns an uncompiled StateGraph you must compile
from langchain_core.agents import create_agent; it returns a Runnable chain without state
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_agent; it returns an AgentExecutor
from langchain.agents import create_agent; it returns a compiled LangGraph graph
objective.explanation: In LangChain v1, create_agent lives in langchain.agents and returns a compiled LangGraph graph. AgentExecutor is the older API, and you do not compile the result yourself.

objective.question: Your agent is compiled with InMemorySaver. A tester calls agent.invoke({"messages": [...]}) twice with no config, and the second call has no memory of the first. What is the most likely cause?
options: The calls did not pass config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "..."}}, so the checkpointer cannot save or load state
create_agent ignores checkpointers unless SummarizationMiddleware is added
InMemorySaver needs a store=InMemoryStore() to save messages
InMemorySaver only works inside the Agent Server
objective.explanation: The checkpointer keys saved state by thread_id, so without it nothing is saved or resumed. A store is for long-term cross-thread memory, and middleware is not required for checkpointing.

objective.question: Your graph paused at an interrupt() on thread_id "order-42". The reviewer approves. How do you continue the run correctly?
options: Call invoke(Command(resume=value), config) with thread_id "order-42"
Call invoke(Command(goto="END")) on any thread
Call graph.update_state with the approval and start a fresh thread
Call invoke with the original input on a new thread_id
objective.explanation: An interrupt is resumed by passing Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, so the checkpointer can load the paused state. A new thread has no paused state to resume.

objective.question: A node first writes an audit row to a database, then calls interrupt() for approval. After resume, you see two audit rows for one request. Why?
options: On resume the interrupted node re-runs from its start, so code before interrupt() runs again
LangSmith tracing re-executes side effects
Command(resume=...) always replays the whole graph from START
The checkpointer duplicates writes on resume
objective.explanation: On resume, the interrupted node runs again from its first line, so the side effect before interrupt() repeats. The fix is to make that code idempotent or move it after the interrupt or into a separate node. The graph does not restart from START.

objective.question: You want a human to approve, edit or reject every send_email tool call. Which configuration matches LangChain v1?
options: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(tools=["send_email"], mode="approve")
PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="approve")
create_agent(..., interrupt_before=["send_email"]) with no checkpointer
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={"send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}})
objective.explanation: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware takes interrupt_on, which maps tool names to their allowed decisions. It also needs a checkpointer to pause and resume. PIIMiddleware handles redaction, not approval.

objective.question: Your capstone runs locally but no traces appear in LangSmith. Which environment setup is required?
options: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY set
LANGGRAPH_TRACE=1
OPENAI_API_KEY and LANGSMITH_PROJECT only
LANGCHAIN_DEBUG=true only
objective.explanation: Tracing needs LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and a valid LANGSMITH_API_KEY. A project name is optional, and the other variables do not turn on LangSmith tracing.

objective.question: You call evaluate(target, data="capstone-rag-v1", evaluators=[correctness]). What does this produce in LangSmith?
options: An experiment: the target runs on every example in the dataset and the evaluators score the outputs
A prompt version in the Prompt Hub
A monitoring rule that scores live traffic only
A new dataset copied from production traces
objective.explanation: evaluate() runs the target over the dataset's examples and records the scored results as an experiment. You can then compare experiments side by side. It does not create datasets or online rules.

objective.question: You want an LLM-as-judge correctness evaluator with minimal custom code. Which option is correct?
options: from openevals.llm import create_llm_as_judge, and use CORRECTNESS_PROMPT from openevals.prompts
Use HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with a judge model
LangChain v1 has no LLM-as-judge support
from langsmith import CORRECTNESS_PROMPT and pass it to evaluate() directly
objective.explanation: openevals provides create_llm_as_judge and ready-made prompts such as CORRECTNESS_PROMPT. The resulting evaluator is passed in evaluators=[...]. Middleware is not an evaluation tool.

objective.question: You want to inspect and step through your local agent visually in LangSmith Studio. What do you need?
options: A langgraph.json config pointing to your graph, then run langgraph dev with the LangGraph CLI
Export the flow to Langflow and open it there
Only the LangSmith API key; Studio finds Python files automatically
Deploy to production first; Studio cannot connect to local agents
objective.explanation: Studio connects to a local agent server started with langgraph dev. That server reads langgraph.json to find your graphs and dependencies. Langflow is a separate tool.

objective.question: While debugging, you call list(graph.get_state_history(config)) for one thread. Which element is the most recent checkpoint?
options: The first element, because the history is returned newest first
It is random; you must sort by step
There is only ever one checkpoint per thread
The last element
objective.explanation: get_state_history returns checkpoints newest first, so index 0 is the latest. A thread keeps many checkpoints, one per super-step, which makes time travel possible.

objective.question: Your capstone uses a main agent that calls a research subagent and a drafting subagent as tools. Where should the checkpointer go, and which pattern is current?
options: Put the checkpointer only on the subagents, because they hold the state
Avoid checkpointers in multi-agent designs
Put the checkpointer only on the outermost main agent, and wrap the worker subagents as tools (the subagents pattern)
Give every subagent its own checkpointer and use langgraph-supervisor
objective.explanation: Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer. The current pattern is a main create_agent whose tools wrap the worker subagents. langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained.

objective.question: An interviewer asks which certificate you hold for Langflow. What is the accurate answer?
options: Langflow has no official certification; my proof is a published flow built from the official docs and tutorials
Langflow certification is part of the LangSmith course
The LangChain Academy course certificate covers Langflow
The official Langflow Professional certificate
objective.explanation: Langflow is a separate open-source visual builder with no official certification. A working, published flow is the honest proof. The LangChain Academy courses cover LangChain, LangGraph and LangSmith, not Langflow.

objective.question: Your capstone agent handles long support chats. What does this middleware configuration do?

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import SummarizationMiddleware

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1",
    tools=[search_docs],
    middleware=[
        SummarizationMiddleware(
            model="openai:gpt-4.1-mini",
            trigger=("tokens", 4000),
            keep=("messages", 20),
        )
    ],
)

options: Every response from the agent is capped at 4,000 tokens, and only 20 tool calls are allowed per thread.
The agent summarises each user message into 20 words before it sends the message to the main model.
After 20 messages, the thread is deleted from the checkpointer and a fresh 4,000-token context is started.
When the conversation reaches about 4,000 tokens, older messages are summarised by the given model and the most recent 20 messages are kept as they are.
objective.explanation: The trigger sets when summarisation starts (a token threshold) and keep sets how much recent history stays untouched. The middleware does not cap output length, limit tool calls or delete threads.

objective.question: A bank requires that customer email addresses never reach the LLM provider. You add the middleware below. What is the behaviour?

code.code:
from langchain.agents.middleware import PIIMiddleware

agent = create_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=tools,
    middleware=[PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True)],
)

options: Emails are encrypted in the trace but are still sent to the model in plain text.
Only emails that appear in tool outputs are redacted; user input is left unchanged.
The agent refuses to run and raises an error whenever the input contains an email.
Emails in the input are detected and redacted before the model sees them.
objective.explanation: PIIMiddleware with strategy="redact" and apply_to_input=True replaces detected emails in the input before the model call. It does not block the request or encrypt traces, and this setting targets input rather than only tool outputs.

objective.question: Your agent must remember a user's preferred language across many separate conversations. Each conversation already uses its own thread_id. Which design fits LangGraph best?
options: Reuse one thread_id for all conversations of the same user, so the checkpointer keeps everything.
Put the preference into the system prompt by reading graph.get_state_history() on every call.
Add a second checkpointer, one for preferences and one for messages.
Compile with a store (for example InMemoryStore during development) and save the preference there, keyed by the user rather than the thread.
objective.explanation: A checkpointer saves per-thread state, while a store holds long-term memory shared across threads. Reusing one thread mixes unrelated conversations, scanning state history is the wrong tool, and two checkpointers is not a supported pattern.

objective.question: This graph fails when you compile or invoke it, with an error about a missing entry point. What is the fix?

code.code:
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("retrieve", retrieve)
builder.add_node("generate", generate)
builder.add_edge("retrieve", "generate")
builder.add_edge("generate", END)
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

options: Remove the checkpointer, because checkpointers need a conditional edge.
Rename the node "retrieve" to "__start__".
Call graph.invoke with {"configurable": {"entry": "retrieve"}}.
Add builder.add_edge(START, "retrieve") so the graph knows where to begin.
objective.explanation: A StateGraph needs an edge from START to define where execution begins. The checkpointer is unrelated, renaming nodes to reserved names is wrong, and no entry key exists in the config.

objective.question: In LangSmith traces, your agent answers policy questions from its own knowledge and never calls the RAG tool below. What is the most likely cause?
options: The @tool decorator only works on async functions.
RAG tools must be passed through middleware, not through the tools list.
Tools that return strings are ignored by create_agent.
The tool name and docstring are too vague, so the model cannot tell when to use it. Give it a clear name and a description of what it searches and when to call it.
objective.explanation: The model chooses tools from their names, descriptions and arguments. A clear name like search_hr_policies, a useful docstring and a system prompt that says when to search usually fix this. The other options describe restrictions that do not exist.

objective.question: During evaluation runs, one example makes your agent loop between the model and a failing tool, and token costs spike. Which change addresses this most directly with LangChain v1 built-ins?
options: Remove the checkpointer so the loop cannot save state.
Turn off LANGSMITH_TRACING to reduce token usage.
Increase the SummarizationMiddleware trigger so the loop has more context.
Add the built-in model call limit middleware (and tool retry middleware with sensible retries) so a run stops after a bounded number of model calls.
objective.explanation: LangChain v1 ships middleware for model call limits and tool retry, which bound runaway loops. Removing persistence or tracing does not stop the loop, and more context does not fix a failing tool.

objective.question: You deploy your capstone on the Agent Server. Your code still compiles the graph with checkpointer=InMemorySaver(). What should you do?
options: Keep InMemorySaver, because the Agent Server has no persistence of its own.
Replace thread_id with a user_id, because the Agent Server ignores threads.
Move the checkpointer onto each subagent instead of the main agent.
Rely on the Agent Server, which handles persistence automatically, and do not hard-code an in-memory checkpointer for deployment.
objective.explanation: The Agent Server provides persistence, so an in-memory saver is only for local development and would lose state on restart. Threads are still used, and only the outermost graph should carry persistence.

objective.question: Put these human-approval steps in the correct order for an agent built with create_agent and HumanInTheLoopMiddleware: (A) the reviewer decides; (B) the model proposes a send_email tool call; (C) the client sends Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id; (D) the middleware interrupts and the checkpointer saves state; (E) the tool runs, or is skipped, based on the decision.
options: B, A, D, C, E
B, D, C, A, E
D, B, A, E, C
B, D, A, C, E
objective.explanation: The model proposes the call first. The middleware then interrupts and the checkpointer saves state. The human decides, the client resumes on the same thread_id, and only then does the tool run or get skipped. The other orders either resume before a decision exists or run the tool before approval.

objective.question: A teammate wrote this resume code. The reviewer clicks Approve, but the agent behaves like a brand-new conversation. What is the mistake?
options: invoke cannot accept a Command; only stream_events can
The decision type must be "approved", not "approve"
A new uuid is generated, so the resume targets an empty thread instead of the paused one
Command must be imported from langchain.agents
objective.explanation: Resume only works on the thread_id that holds the saved interrupt. A fresh uuid points at a thread with no checkpoint, so the paused run is never continued. invoke does accept a Command, and the import location and the decision string are not the problem.

objective.question: Your evaluate() experiment works for policy Q&A examples. Examples like "email the customer their refund status" return no final answer, and the correctness scores for them are near zero. What is the most likely cause?
options: LangSmith datasets cannot contain imperative instructions
evaluate() runs examples without the agent's tools
Those examples hit the HumanInTheLoopMiddleware interrupt on send_email, and the target function never resumes it
The LLM-as-judge prompt cannot grade email content
objective.explanation: The agent pauses at the approval interrupt, and nothing in the target resumes it. The run therefore ends without a final message. The fix is to keep the eval set on retrieval Q&A, or to handle approvals inside the target function. Datasets and evaluate() have no such limits.

objective.question: Spot the mistake in this subagents design.

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

researcher = create_agent(model, tools=[search_docs],
                          checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

@tool
def research(question: str) -> str:
    """Research a question using internal docs."""
    result = researcher.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}]})
    return result["messages"][-1].content

main = create_agent(model, tools=[research],
                    checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

options: The inner researcher subagent has its own checkpointer; only the outermost graph should have one
The main agent should be built with langgraph-supervisor
Subagents cannot be called inside a @tool function
The research tool must return a dict, not a string
objective.explanation: In the subagents pattern, only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer. Giving the inner subagent its own checkpointer is the documented trap. Wrapping a subagent in a tool that returns a string is the intended pattern, and langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained.

objective.question: Approvals never trigger, and emails go out without review. Which line explains it?
options: The interrupt_on key "send_email" does not match the tool name "send_mail", so that tool is never intercepted
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware only works with create_deep_agent
allowed_decisions must contain only "approve"
The checkpointer must be passed to the middleware
objective.explanation: interrupt_on is keyed by tool name. The tool is named send_mail, so no rule applies to it and it runs freely. The other options describe requirements that do not exist.

objective.question: A loan-support agent has three requirements: mask customer email addresses before they reach the model, require approval for the issue_refund tool, and stop runaway loops. Which middleware set meets all three with built-ins?
options: PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True), HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={"issue_refund": {...}}), ModelCallLimitMiddleware
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware for all tools, plus a longer system prompt asking the model not to read emails
PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact"), ToolRetryMiddleware, LLMToolSelectorMiddleware
SummarizationMiddleware, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, ModelFallbackMiddleware
objective.explanation: PII redaction on input covers the masking requirement. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware keyed on issue_refund covers approval, and a model call limit stops loops. Summarization, fallback, retry and tool selection address other problems, and a system prompt is not enforcement.

objective.question: A node calls interrupt({"draft": draft}) and is later resumed with Command(resume="looks good"). What happens on resume?
options: The node re-runs from its start, and when it reaches interrupt() again, the call returns "looks good"
The node is skipped, and "looks good" is written into state automatically
The whole graph restarts from START with the resume value as the new input
Execution continues on the line after interrupt(), and interrupt() returns None
objective.explanation: On resume, the interrupted node runs again from the top. The interrupt() call then returns the resume value instead of pausing. The run does not restart the graph, and the value is not written into state automatically.

objective.question: During your interview demo, you restart the Python process while an approval is pending. After the restart, resuming on the same thread_id finds nothing to resume. What is the cause?
options: InMemorySaver keeps checkpoints only in process memory, so the restart lost the saved interrupt
Command(resume=...) only works inside LangSmith Studio
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware clears state on every new process
thread_id values expire after a few minutes
objective.explanation: InMemorySaver is in-memory, so its checkpoints disappear when the process exits. Use a persistent checkpointer, or deploy on the Agent Server, which handles persistence automatically. Thread IDs do not expire, and resume is not tied to Studio.

objective.question: Two testers use your web demo at the same time and start seeing each other's messages. The backend code is below. What is the cause?
options: Every request uses the same hard-coded thread_id, so both users write to one conversation
InMemorySaver cannot handle more than one request
The messages list must include the full history on every call
The model provider mixes up concurrent requests
objective.explanation: A thread_id identifies one conversation. A shared constant merges all users into a single thread. Generate or look up a thread_id per user session. The other options are not real causes.

objective.question: Put these steps for running a LangSmith evaluation in order: (A) review scores and failing runs in the experiment; (B) create a dataset of examples with inputs and reference outputs; (C) define evaluators such as an openevals LLM-as-judge; (D) write a target function that calls the agent; (E) call evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]).
options: B, E, D, C, A
C, B, E, D, A
B, D, C, E, A
D, C, E, B, A
objective.explanation: You need the dataset first, then a target to run against it, then evaluators, then evaluate() to run the experiment, and finally a review of the results. Calling evaluate() before the target or evaluators exist is impossible.

objective.question: Running langgraph dev fails because it cannot find your graph. Your agent object is called agent in src/app/agent.py. Which langgraph.json is correct?
options: Option C
Option D
Option B
Option A
objective.explanation: The graphs map uses a graph name as the key and a value of the form path:variable. Option B leaves out the variable name, and options C and D use the wrong keys or shapes.

objective.question: Which README excerpt best meets what interviewers expect from a capstone?
options: "Eval: 40-example dataset capstone-rag-v1; evaluators: LLM-as-judge correctness (openevals CORRECTNESS_PROMPT) and a tool-called check; correctness 0.85, tool-called 0.95; experiment link and demo video link below."
"Scores: 100% on all tests." (no dataset or evaluator details)
"We tested many questions manually and the answers looked good. See screenshots."
"The agent is accurate and fast. It uses LangChain, LangGraph and LangSmith. Evaluation was done."
objective.explanation: Interviewers want the dataset size, evaluator names, scores and links they can verify. The other options are either vague or give a number with no method behind it.

objective.question: Your target function for evaluate() is below. Every example after the first gets odd answers that refer to earlier questions. What is the fix?
options: Add SummarizationMiddleware so the history stays short
Run evaluate() with fewer examples
Use a fresh thread_id for each example, for example str(uuid.uuid4()) inside target
Remove the return dict and return the raw result
objective.explanation: A fixed thread_id carries the checkpointed history from one example into the next, so the examples contaminate each other. Each example should run on its own new thread. Summarizing or reducing the examples hides the leak instead of fixing it.

subjective.question: Walk me through the architecture of your capstone agent.
subjective.answer: My capstone is a support agent built with create_agent from langchain.agents, which returns a compiled LangGraph graph. It has three tools. A retrieve_docs tool runs RAG over a vector store of product docs. A lookup_order tool reads order data. A send_email tool takes action. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware guards send_email, so a person can approve, edit or reject each email before it goes out. SummarizationMiddleware keeps long threads within the context budget. The agent is compiled with a checkpointer, and every call passes a thread_id, so conversations persist and interrupts can resume. LANGSMITH_TRACING is on, so every run is traced. I also keep a LangSmith dataset of about 40 questions with reference answers. I run evaluate() against it with a correctness judge and a retrieval check, and I compare experiments whenever I change the prompt or the model. The README contains the diagram, the results and a demo link.
keyPoints: create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph
RAG exposed as a tool alongside action tools
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on risky tools plus a checkpointer and thread_id
LangSmith tracing and an evaluation dataset with evaluate()

subjective.question: Why did you expose RAG as a tool instead of retrieving on every turn?
subjective.answer: Making retrieval a tool lets the model decide when it needs documents. Greetings, follow-ups that the conversation history already answers, and pure action requests skip retrieval. That cuts latency and cost, and it keeps irrelevant chunks out of the context, which can confuse the model. It also allows multi-step behaviour. The agent can retrieve, see the results are weak, and retrieve again with a refined query. The tool description matters a lot, so I state what the corpus contains and when to use it. The trade-off is that the model may skip retrieval when it should not. I watch for that in LangSmith traces, and my evaluation set includes questions that need grounding. If skipping shows up often, I tighten the system prompt or the tool description. For strict compliance use cases, an always-retrieve step in a custom LangGraph node is still a valid choice.
keyPoints: Model decides when to retrieve, which saves cost and latency
Enables iterative, multi-step retrieval
Tool description quality drives correct use
Risk of skipped retrieval is monitored with traces and evals

subjective.question: Explain the full human-approval flow in your agent, from the tool call to the resume.
subjective.answer: The model proposes a send_email tool call. Because send_email is listed in HumanInTheLoopMiddleware's interrupt_on, the middleware pauses the run before the tool executes. The checkpointer saves state under the current thread_id. I drive the graph with stream_events using version="v3", and the stream reports the interruption and its payload. That payload contains the proposed tool call and the allowed decisions, which are approve, edit and reject. My UI shows the email to the reviewer. When the reviewer decides, I call the agent again with Command(resume=...) carrying that decision, on the same thread_id. On approve, the tool runs as proposed. On edit, it runs with the reviewer's changed arguments. On reject, the tool does not run and the model receives that feedback. Without a checkpointer and a thread_id there is nothing to resume, so the checkpointer is mandatory.
keyPoints: interrupt_on with allowed_decisions approve, edit and reject
State saved by the checkpointer under thread_id
Interrupt surfaced through stream_events v3
Resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id

subjective.question: What exactly do the checkpointer and thread_id do, and how would this change in production?
subjective.answer: A checkpointer saves the graph's state at each step. thread_id is the key that groups those checkpoints into one conversation. I pass it as config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "..."}}. Without it the checkpointer cannot save or resume anything. That breaks memory and also breaks human-in-the-loop, because an interrupt has nowhere to resume from. Checkpoints also enable debugging and time travel. graph.get_state_history(config) lists them newest first, so I can inspect the state at any step. In development I use InMemorySaver, which disappears when the process restarts. In production I would use a durable, database-backed checkpointer, or deploy on the Agent Server, which handles persistence automatically. A store such as InMemoryStore is different. It holds long-term memory shared across threads, while the checkpointer holds the state of each thread.
keyPoints: Checkpointer saves state per step and thread_id keys the conversation
No thread_id means no save, no resume and no HITL
get_state_history returns checkpoints newest first
InMemorySaver for dev; durable saver or Agent Server in production; store is cross-thread memory

subjective.question: An interrupted node re-runs from its start when resumed. What problems does this cause and how do you design for it?
subjective.answer: When I resume with Command(resume=...), LangGraph does not continue from the line after interrupt(). It re-runs the whole node, and on this second run interrupt() returns the resume value instead of pausing. Any code before the interrupt therefore runs twice. That includes API calls, database writes, charging a card or sending a notification. To design for this, I place interrupt() at the very top of the node, or I put side effects in a separate node after the approval node. If work must happen before the pause, I make it idempotent, for example with an idempotency key or an upsert. I also avoid expensive LLM calls before an interrupt, because they double the cost. If a node has several interrupts, I keep their order fixed, because resume values are matched by order. I test this by checking traces for duplicate tool spans after resume.
keyPoints: Resume re-runs the node from its start; interrupt() returns the resume value
Code before interrupt runs twice
Put interrupt first or move side effects to separate nodes
Make pre-interrupt work idempotent and keep the order of multiple interrupts stable

subjective.question: A user reports a wrong answer from your agent. How do you use LangSmith to find the cause?
subjective.answer: With LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY set, every run is a trace. I find the run by filtering on thread_id metadata, time or user feedback. I open the trace tree and read it in order. First the model call: did it pick the right tool? Next the retrieve_docs span: what query was sent, and were the returned chunks relevant? Then the final model call: did it use the chunks or ignore them? This quickly shows whether the fault is retrieval, tool choice or generation. For deeper stepping, I run the agent locally with langgraph dev and open it in LangSmith Studio. I then add the failing case to my evaluation dataset with the correct reference answer, so the bug becomes a regression test. After the fix, I run evaluate() again and compare the new experiment with the old one.
keyPoints: Tracing via LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY
Inspect tool choice, retrieval and generation spans to localise the fault
Studio via langgraph dev and langgraph.json for interactive debugging
Add the failure to the dataset and re-run evaluate() to confirm the fix

subjective.question: How did you build the evaluation set for your capstone, and what does each example contain?
subjective.answer: I created a LangSmith dataset of about 40 examples. Each example has inputs, which are the user question, and reference outputs, which are the expected answer and sometimes the expected source document or tool. I covered several categories. There are common questions answerable from the docs, multi-step questions that need retrieval and an order lookup, out-of-scope questions where the right answer is 'I don't know', and adversarial or ambiguous prompts. I also added cases that should trigger send_email, to check that the agent proposes the action rather than doing it silently. I seeded examples from real traces and hand-wrote the edge cases. The dataset is versioned, so results stay comparable over time. I run evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]), where target wraps my agent. Every prompt or model change gets its own named experiment, so I can compare them side by side.
keyPoints: Dataset of examples with inputs and reference outputs
Coverage: happy path, multi-step, out-of-scope, adversarial, action cases
Seed from real traces and add hand-written edge cases
evaluate() creates comparable experiments per change

subjective.question: What are the risks of LLM-as-judge evaluation, and how did you mitigate them?
subjective.answer: I used create_llm_as_judge from openevals with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, comparing outputs to the reference answers. The judge is fast and handles paraphrases well, but it has known risks. It can be inconsistent across runs, it may favour long or confident answers, and it can share blind spots with the model it is judging. To mitigate this, I use a strong judge model and ask for a score with reasoning, so I can audit its decisions. I spot-check a sample of judgements by hand and fix the rubric when the judge and I disagree. I also pair the judge with deterministic code evaluators. Examples are whether the right tool was called, whether a source was cited, and whether out-of-scope questions were refused. These are cheap and exact. Finally, I track trends across experiments rather than trusting one absolute number.
keyPoints: create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT from openevals
Risks: inconsistency, length bias, shared blind spots
Human spot checks and rubric tuning
Combine with deterministic code evaluators and compare experiments

subjective.question: When would you add subagents to the capstone, and how would you structure them?
subjective.answer: I would add subagents when one agent has too many tools or the context becomes crowded. One example is a research worker that does many retrieval rounds, next to a drafting worker that writes emails. The current pattern is a main create_agent whose tools wrap worker subagents. Each worker is its own create_agent with a focused prompt and tool set. The wrapper tool invokes the worker and returns only its final result, which keeps the main agent's context clean. I would not use langgraph-supervisor, because it is no longer actively maintained. Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer, so persistence and interrupts are handled once, at the top. The workers do not get their own. For long-running, file-heavy tasks, create_deep_agent is an option, because it pre-assembles a filesystem, summarization, subagents and prompt caching. For a demo, I keep it optional, because a single agent is easier to explain.
keyPoints: Use subagents when tools or context overload a single agent
Main create_agent with tools wrapping worker subagents
Do not use langgraph-supervisor; it is no longer actively maintained
Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer; create_deep_agent for long tasks

subjective.question: What goes into your capstone README, and why does it matter in an interview?
subjective.answer: The README is my interview artefact, so a reviewer should understand the project in two minutes. It opens with the problem and a one-line summary. Next comes an architecture diagram showing the user, the create_agent graph, its middleware, the tools (RAG retriever, order lookup, send_email with human approval), the checkpointer and LangSmith. Then there are setup steps: the required environment variables, including LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY, and how to run it with langgraph dev. The evaluation section names the dataset and its size, lists the evaluators, and shows a results table comparing at least two experiments. A design decisions section explains why RAG is a tool, how interrupt and resume work, and the known limitations. It ends with a demo link, either a short video or a hosted app, plus a sample trace screenshot. Evidence-backed numbers make interview answers credible and specific.
keyPoints: Problem statement and architecture diagram
Setup with env vars and the langgraph dev command
Evaluation results comparing experiments
Design decisions, limitations and a demo link

subjective.question: How does your UI drive the agent and detect that it is waiting for human approval?
subjective.answer: I drive the graph with stream_events(..., version="v3"), which is the recommended approach. It streams model tokens, tool start and end events, and state updates. I can therefore show the reply as it is generated, along with progress such as 'searching docs'. When HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses on send_email, the stream reports the interruption through stream.interrupted, and stream.interrupts holds the payload with the proposed action and the allowed decisions. The UI then switches to an approval card with approve, edit and reject buttons. The click sends Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, and streaming continues. Because state lives in the checkpointer, the reviewer does not have to answer immediately. The thread can resume later, even from another session, as long as the same thread_id is used and the checkpointer is durable.
keyPoints: stream_events with version="v3" is the recommended driver
stream.interrupted and stream.interrupts surface pauses
UI renders the approval and resumes with Command(resume=...)
Durable checkpointer allows a delayed resume on the same thread_id

subjective.question: How do you present your certificates and Langflow work honestly on your CV and in interviews?
subjective.answer: I list the LangChain Academy courses I completed: LangChain, LangGraph and LangSmith. They are free, self-paced courses with notebooks and videos. I describe them as course completions, not professional certifications, and I back them with my capstone, because the project is the real proof. For Langflow, I say plainly that there is no official certification. Instead, I show a published flow that I built using the official docs and tutorials, for example a visual prototype of the same RAG assistant. I explain that I use Langflow to prototype and demo ideas quickly with components, test them in the Playground, and call the flow through its API. I then move to Python with create_agent and LangGraph when I need finer control, testing and evaluation. Interviewers value accuracy, so I never invent credentials.
keyPoints: LangChain Academy courses are free, self-paced and course-based
The capstone is the main proof of skill
Langflow has no official certification; show a published flow
Langflow for visual prototyping; Python LangGraph for production control

subjective.question: Explain what this agent setup does, step by step, and how you would test each part before your demo.

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import (
    SummarizationMiddleware, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, PIIMiddleware)
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1",
    tools=[search_policies, send_email],
    system_prompt="Answer HR questions using search_policies. Cite sources.",
    middleware=[
        PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True),
        SummarizationMiddleware(model="openai:gpt-4.1-mini",
            trigger=("tokens", 4000), keep=("messages", 20)),
        HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={
            "send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}}),
    ],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

subjective.answer: create_agent builds a compiled LangGraph agent that loops between the model and two tools. search_policies is the RAG tool. send_email is the risky action. PIIMiddleware redacts emails in the input before the model sees them. SummarizationMiddleware compresses old history once the thread passes about 4,000 tokens and keeps the last 20 messages. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses before every send_email call so a reviewer can approve, edit or reject it. InMemorySaver stores state per thread_id, which makes that pause and resume possible. To test it, I send an input with an email and check in the LangSmith trace that it is redacted. I run a long synthetic chat and confirm a summary appears. I trigger send_email and check the run interrupts, then resume with approve, edit and reject on the same thread_id. Finally, I run the evaluation dataset to confirm the answers still cite sources.
keyPoints: create_agent returns a compiled graph; the tools are RAG plus a risky action
PII redaction on input, and summarisation with token trigger and message keep
HITL interrupt on send_email with approve, edit and reject
Checkpointer plus thread_id enables pause and resume
A concrete test for each feature using traces and the evaluation set

subjective.question: Your RAG tool is being called, but answers are still wrong because the retrieved chunks are irrelevant. How do you diagnose and fix this?
subjective.answer: First I open the failing run in LangSmith and look at the tool span. It shows the exact query the model sent and the chunks that came back. That tells me whether the problem is the query, the retrieval or the generation. If the model rewrote the question badly, I improve the tool description and the system prompt, or I let the tool accept the user's wording. If the query is fine but the chunks are poor, I check chunk size and overlap, the embedding model, metadata filters and the k value. Often I need smaller chunks with section titles attached. If good chunks came back but the answer ignored them, it is a prompting or grounding issue. I add the failing cases to my LangSmith dataset. Then I separate retrieval checks, such as whether the expected source was retrieved, from answer correctness, and I re-run evaluate() after each change to confirm the fix.
keyPoints: Use the tool span in the trace to see the query and the returned chunks
Isolate the failure: query formulation, retrieval quality or generation
Fixes: chunking, embeddings, metadata filters, k, tool description
Add failures to the dataset and measure retrieval and answer quality separately
Re-run the experiment to confirm the improvement

subjective.question: A final-answer correctness score is not enough for a multi-step agent. What else would you evaluate in your capstone, and how?
subjective.answer: For a multi-step agent, the path matters as much as the answer. I add trajectory checks. Did the agent call the RAG tool when the question needed internal data? Did it avoid calling send_email when it should only answer? Did it stay within a reasonable number of steps? I write these as simple code evaluators that read the run's messages and tool calls, because deterministic checks are cheaper and more reliable than a judge. I keep LLM-as-judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT for answer quality against reference outputs. For human approval, I test that an interrupt happens for every risky tool call, and that a reject leads to a sensible reply instead of the action. I also track latency and token cost from the traces. All of these run as one evaluate() experiment, so I can compare versions side by side.
keyPoints: Trajectory checks: correct tool selection and no unwanted actions
Step-count, latency and cost from traces
Deterministic code evaluators where possible, LLM judge for answer quality
Verify interrupts fire for risky tools and that the reject path behaves well
Compare versions as experiments on the same dataset

subjective.question: The reviewer chooses "edit" or "reject" on a send_email call. What should your agent do in each case, and what bugs have you seen here?
subjective.answer: On approve, the tool runs with the original arguments. On edit, the reviewer's changed arguments replace the model's, such as a corrected recipient or body, and the tool runs with those. On reject, the tool does not run. The agent should get feedback that the action was declined and then tell the user, or ask what to change, instead of silently retrying. In every case I resume on the same thread_id. Common bugs include resuming on a new thread_id, which loses the paused state. Another is a UI that does not check for interrupts and shows the run as finished. A third is the model trying the same email again straight after a reject. Side effects placed before the pause can also run twice, because the node re-runs from its start on resume. I cover all three decisions in tests and confirm them in the LangSmith traces.
keyPoints: Approve runs the original call; edit runs with the reviewer's arguments; reject skips the tool
Always resume on the same thread_id
After a reject, the agent informs the user instead of retrying blindly
Watch for duplicate side effects because the node re-runs on resume
Test all three decisions and check the traces

subjective.question: Would you build your capstone with create_agent or create_deep_agent? Justify the choice.
subjective.answer: For my capstone I used create_agent. The task is bounded: answer questions with RAG, and send an email only after human approval. A single agent loop with a few middleware is easy to explain, trace and evaluate. create_deep_agent is meant for long-running, open-ended tasks. It pre-assembles a filesystem for intermediate work, summarisation, subagents and prompt caching. I would switch to it if the capstone grew into multi-hour research, such as reading many documents, writing drafts to files and delegating sections to subagents. That extra machinery adds behaviour I would need to understand and evaluate, so I avoid it when the task does not need it. In an interview, I explain that I picked the simplest design that met the requirements, and I describe the signals that would make me move to a deep agent.
keyPoints: create_agent suits bounded tasks and is easier to trace and evaluate
create_deep_agent bundles filesystem, summarisation, subagents and prompt caching
Switch for long-running, multi-file or delegated work
Avoid unnecessary complexity and justify the choice by requirements

subjective.question: You prototyped the agent visually in Langflow first. How do you move from that prototype to the Python capstone, and what do you show from Langflow?
subjective.answer: I used Langflow to try ideas quickly. I connected a loader, a vector store, a retriever and a model as components, then tested prompts in the Playground. This helped me choose the chunk settings, the prompt and the tool layout before I wrote any code. For the capstone, I rebuilt the logic in Python with create_agent, a retriever tool and HumanInTheLoopMiddleware. Code gives me version control, unit tests, checkpointers, LangSmith evaluation and a clean deployment path. I keep the Langflow flow as a separate artefact. I publish it or export it and call it through its API, and I link it from the README with a short note on what I learned from it. In interviews, I am clear that Langflow has no official certification. My evidence is the published flow and how I used it to make design decisions.
keyPoints: Langflow is for rapid visual prototyping with components and the Playground
Port the validated design into Python with create_agent and middleware
Python adds tests, version control, evaluation and deployment
Publish or share the flow and link it in the README
Be honest that Langflow has no official certification

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: "Your agent is slow and expensive. Use your traces to make it cheaper without losing quality." How do you answer?
subjective.answer: I start from data, not guesses. In LangSmith, I sort runs by latency and token usage and open the worst ones to see where time and tokens go. That might be long histories, large retrieved contexts, repeated tool calls or retries. Then I apply targeted fixes. SummarizationMiddleware keeps context small in long threads. I reduce k or chunk size in the RAG tool. I add the model call limit middleware to stop loops, and tool retry middleware with sane limits so failures do not cascade. I may use a cheaper model for summarisation, or model fallback middleware for resilience. For agents with many tools, the LLM tool selection middleware can shrink the tool list per call. After each change, I re-run evaluate() on the same dataset and compare experiments. That way I only keep changes that cut cost or latency while correctness stays at the same level.
keyPoints: Find the hotspots from trace latency and token data
Fixes: summarisation, a smaller retrieval context, call limits, tool retry
Cheaper models where suitable; tool selection for large toolsets
Validate every change with an evaluation experiment
Keep only changes that hold quality steady

subjective.question: Case study: an insurance firm wants an agent that answers claim-policy questions from 2,000 PDF pages. It must get human approval before any payout above a threshold, never send customer emails to the model provider, be traceable, and show measured quality. Design it with the LangChain v1 stack.
subjective.answer: I would use create_agent with a retrieval tool, search_policies, over a vector index of the chunked PDFs. The tool returns passages with source and page, so answers can cite their source. Payouts go through an approve_payout tool. For the approval rule, I would interrupt on approve_payout with HumanInTheLoopMiddleware. To apply the threshold, I would put the amount check inside the tool, or use a custom middleware hook, because HumanInTheLoopMiddleware applies per tool. PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True) masks addresses before the model sees them. A persistent checkpointer, with a thread_id per claim, lets approvals survive restarts. I would add a model call limit to stop loops. For tracing, I would set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY. For quality, I would build a LangSmith dataset of policy questions with reference answers and citations. I would run evaluate() with an LLM-as-judge correctness evaluator plus a tool-called check, and report the scores in the README.
keyPoints: RAG exposed as a tool that returns sources
HITL on the payout tool, with the threshold logic placed deliberately
PIIMiddleware on input, plus a persistent checkpointer with a thread_id per claim
Tracing env vars and a dataset-based evaluate() with named evaluators

subjective.question: After the reviewer clicks Approve, your agent replies "Sure, how can I help?" and never sends the email. Here is the handler. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The thread_id is correct, but the handler sends a new user message instead of resuming the interrupt. The graph treats "approve" as fresh input, so the pending send_email tool call is never answered. The model then just replies to the word "approve". The fix is to pass a Command: agent.invoke(Command(resume={"decisions": [{"type": "approve"}]}), config=config) on the same thread_id. That supplies the decision the HumanInTheLoopMiddleware is waiting for, and the tool then runs. I would also check that the UI reads the interrupt payload, so it knows which tool call it is approving. I would add a test: start a run that triggers send_email, assert that the run is interrupted, resume with approve, and assert that the tool executed exactly once. In LangSmith, the trace should show one continuous run on that thread, not a new turn.
keyPoints: A new user message is not a resume
Use Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id
The pending tool call is only answered by the resume decision
Add a test asserting the tool ran once after the resume

subjective.question: Compare using HumanInTheLoopMiddleware in create_agent with writing your own interrupt() call inside a custom StateGraph node. Which is better for the capstone, and when would you choose the other?
subjective.answer: For the capstone, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware is better. It intercepts tool calls by name and supports approve, edit and reject decisions out of the box. It also works with create_agent, which already returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so I write less code and have fewer resume bugs. I would write my own interrupt() in a StateGraph node when approval is not tied to one tool call. Examples are reviewing a whole draft plan before several steps, or approving a step in a fixed pipeline. A custom node is also useful when the approval payload needs a specific shape for a custom UI. The trade-off is that I own the semantics myself. The node re-runs from its start on resume, so any non-idempotent work must come after interrupt() or live in a separate node. I must also validate the resume value myself. In an interview, I would say I used the built-in and know when to drop down a level.
keyPoints: The middleware covers per-tool approve, edit and reject with little code
A custom interrupt() suits approvals not tied to a single tool call
With a custom node, you own the re-run-from-start and validation
Choose based on where the decision sits in the flow

subjective.question: Order the steps to take your capstone from an empty repo to an interview-ready demo in Week 10, and justify the order.
subjective.answer: First, scope the agent and write a small eval set of real questions, so I know what "working" means. Second, build the RAG tool and test it on its own. Third, wrap it with create_agent and a system prompt, and check that the model actually calls the tool. Fourth, turn on LangSmith tracing early, so every later bug is visible. Fifth, add the checkpointer, thread_id handling and HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on send_email, and test the interrupt and resume path. Sixth, add langgraph.json and inspect the agent in Studio with langgraph dev. Seventh, run evaluate() on the dataset, fix the failures and re-run to compare experiments. Eighth, write the README with the diagram, scores, experiment link and demo link. Last, record a backup demo video. Tracing comes early because it makes debugging cheap. Evaluation comes before the README so that the numbers are real. Finishing the Academy courses runs alongside all of this.
keyPoints: Define scope and eval questions first
Build and test the tool before the agent
Turn on tracing early, then add HITL and the checkpointer, with tests
Evaluate before writing the README; keep a backup demo

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this multi-agent plan from a teammate's design document, and rewrite it.

code.code:
- Use langgraph-supervisor to route between research_agent and writer_agent
- Compile research_agent with its own InMemorySaver
- Compile writer_agent with its own InMemorySaver
- Compile supervisor with InMemorySaver
- Each agent gets a separate thread_id per request

subjective.answer: There are three problems. First, langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained, so new work should not depend on it. Second, the inner agents each have their own checkpointer. Only the outermost graph should have one, otherwise state is split and harder to resume. Third, separate thread_ids per agent break the link between one user conversation and its saved state. The rewrite: build research_agent and writer_agent with create_agent and no checkpointer. Wrap each in a tool with a clear docstring, for example research(question) and draft(brief), each returning a concise string. Then create the main agent with create_agent, tools=[research, draft], and a single checkpointer. The client passes one thread_id per user conversation. Approvals, such as HITL on send_email, live on the main agent, so the interrupt happens on the thread being checkpointed. Traces in LangSmith will then show the subagent calls nested under the main run.
keyPoints: Do not build on langgraph-supervisor
Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer
Wrap subagents as tools of a main create_agent
Use one thread_id per user conversation

subjective.question: For your capstone eval set, which evaluator would you use for each check, and why? (1) Did the agent call the RAG tool? (2) Does the answer cite a source? (3) Is the answer factually correct against a reference?
subjective.answer: For (1), I would use a deterministic code evaluator that inspects the run's messages or trace for a tool call named search_policies. The answer is binary, so an LLM judge would add cost and noise. For (2), a simple code check also works if I enforce a citation format, such as a bracketed source ID that matches the retrieved document IDs. If the format is loose, a small LLM judge is acceptable. For (3), I would use an LLM-as-judge from openevals with create_llm_as_judge and CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, comparing the output with the reference answer. Wording varies too much for exact match. The rule is to use the cheapest reliable evaluator for each question. Code checks are fast, cheap and repeatable. LLM judges handle meaning but need spot-checking against human labels. All three would run in one evaluate() call, so the README reports three separate scores, not one blended number.
keyPoints: Use deterministic checks for tool use and format
Use an LLM-as-judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT for semantic correctness
Pick the cheapest reliable evaluator per check
Report scores separately in the README

subjective.question: You changed the chunk size from 1,000 to 300 tokens, re-ran evaluate(), and correctness dropped from 0.82 to 0.70. Walk through how you find out why.
subjective.answer: I would compare the two experiments on the same dataset in LangSmith and sort by examples whose score dropped. For each regressed example, I would open the trace and look at the RAG tool's input and output. Was the query the same? Did the retrieved chunks still contain the answer, or is the fact now split across two small chunks, with only one returned? I would also check whether the model called the tool at all, and whether it called it more often with worse queries. If the cause is a split context, I would raise the number of retrieved chunks, add overlap or go back to a larger size. Then I would re-run the same dataset and compare again. I would also check whether the judge itself is noisy, by reading a few failures by hand. I change one variable at a time, so the cause stays clear. I would record the finding and both scores in the README.
keyPoints: Compare experiments on the same dataset and focus on regressions
Inspect the retrieval tool's input and output in traces
Form a hypothesis such as split context and change one variable
Re-run, compare and check judge noise by hand

subjective.question: Your interview demo is live over a video call. List what can go wrong and how you prepare for each.
subjective.answer: The model provider may be slow or down. ModelFallbackMiddleware switches to a backup model, and I keep a recorded demo video linked in the README. Restarting the app can lose a pending approval if I use InMemorySaver, so I use a persistent checkpointer or the Agent Server. I also never restart mid-demo. The model may skip the RAG tool on an unusual question, so I prepare three rehearsed questions that I know call the tool, and keep the system prompt explicit about when to use it. The approval UI might miss the interrupt, so I test the full interrupt and resume path with a script beforehand. Network or API key issues are handled by checking environment variables, including LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY, before the call. Finally, I keep a LangSmith trace and an experiment page open in tabs. If something fails live, I explain it using the trace, which shows real debugging skill.
keyPoints: Model fallback middleware and a recorded backup video
Persistent checkpointing so approvals survive restarts
Rehearsed questions and a tested interrupt and resume path
Traces open in tabs to explain any live failure

subjective.question: Compare SummarizationMiddleware with a LangGraph store for these two needs: keeping a 200-message support chat within the context window, and remembering a customer's account tier across all future chats.
subjective.answer: They solve different problems. SummarizationMiddleware works inside one thread. When the configured trigger is reached, for example a token count, it summarizes older messages and keeps a recent window. That fits the 200-message chat, and the checkpointer stores the summarized history under that thread_id. It does not help a new conversation, because a new thread_id starts empty. The account tier is long-term, cross-thread memory, so it belongs in a store, such as InMemoryStore in development or a persistent store in production. It should be keyed by a user namespace, and read at the start of each conversation or through a tool. Putting the tier only in chat history is fragile, because summarization may drop it. Putting the whole chat in the store is also wrong, because the store is for durable facts, not transcripts. So I would use both: the checkpointer plus summarization for short-term memory, and the store for user facts.
keyPoints: Summarization manages context within a single thread
A store holds cross-thread, per-user facts
Summarization can drop details, so durable facts go to the store
Use both together, each for its own job

subjective.question: Your eval set must include some questions that lead to send_email. How do you write the target function so the experiment completes, and what do you measure?
subjective.answer: The target function must handle the approval itself. I give each example a fresh thread_id. I invoke the agent with the question, then check whether the run is interrupted. If it is, I read the interrupt payload to see the proposed tool call and its arguments. I then resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, using a fixed policy. For example, I approve in a happy-path experiment, or reject to test how the agent handles refusals. To avoid real emails, the send_email tool in the eval environment is a stub that records its calls. The target returns the final answer plus the proposed email arguments. Evaluators can then check two things: did the agent propose an email when it should, and were the recipient and body correct against the reference outputs. Keeping pure retrieval Q&A in a separate dataset keeps those scores clean and easy to compare.
keyPoints: Use a fresh thread_id per example and detect the interrupt
Resume with Command on the same thread using a fixed policy
Stub send_email to avoid side effects
Evaluate the proposed tool arguments; keep a separate RAG dataset

subjective.question: Spot the weaknesses in this README section and rewrite it the way you would ship it.

code.code:
## Evaluation
We evaluated the agent thoroughly and it performs very well.
Human approval works. Tracing is enabled.
See the code for details.

subjective.answer: It has no numbers, no method and no links, so an interviewer cannot verify anything. I would rewrite it like this. "Evaluation: a LangSmith dataset capstone-rag-v1 with 40 examples, of which 30 are policy Q&A and 10 are out-of-scope refusals, each with a reference answer. Evaluators: an openevals LLM-as-judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, plus a code check that the search tool was called. Results: correctness 0.85, tool-called 0.95. Main failure: multi-part questions, fixed by retrieving more chunks, which raised correctness from 0.78. Links: the LangSmith experiment comparison and the demo video. Human approval: send_email is interrupted with approve, edit and reject, and a test covers the resume path. Tracing: an example trace link." I would also add a diagram showing the client, agent, tools, checkpointer and LangSmith. Numbers alone, with no denominator, invite questions, so I always give the dataset size and the evaluator names.
keyPoints: The original has no dataset size, evaluators, scores or links
Name the dataset, its size and its composition
Report scores per evaluator and a before/after fix
Link the experiment, a trace and the demo; add a diagram

subjective.question: You added ToolRetryMiddleware, and a customer received the same email twice after a timeout. Explain the cause and how you would redesign the tool.
subjective.answer: The timeout happened after the email provider had accepted the message but before the tool returned. The retry middleware saw a failure and called send_email again. Retries are safe only for idempotent tools. Sending email is not idempotent. The same risk appears with interrupts: a node re-runs from its start on resume, so side effects placed before interrupt() repeat. To redesign, I would give each send an idempotency key derived from the thread_id and the tool call ID. The tool first checks a sent-log for that key, and returns the stored result if the key already exists. If the provider supports idempotency keys, I would pass the key through to it as well. I would also scope retries to read-only tools, such as the RAG search, and keep send_email out of automatic retry, or retry only on errors that clearly happen before sending. Then I would add a test that simulates a timeout and asserts that the provider received one send.
keyPoints: Retries repeat non-idempotent side effects
Re-runs after interrupts carry the same risk
Use an idempotency key from the thread and tool call ID, with a sent-log
Limit retries to safe tools and test the timeout case

subjective.question: An interviewer gives you this case: "Two days before launch, Studio shows the agent working, but in production users say approvals hang forever." How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: Studio works with langgraph dev, which handles persistence for the local run. So I would suspect the production wiring rather than the agent logic. First, I would check that the production client sends a stable thread_id per conversation, and reuses it on resume. Second, I would confirm that the client detects the pause. For example, when driving the graph with stream_events(..., version="v3"), it must check whether the stream was interrupted and show the approval UI. Otherwise the run waits silently. Third, I would confirm that the approve button sends Command(resume=...), not a new user message. Fourth, I would check persistence. If the code uses InMemorySaver behind several workers or after restarts, the interrupt may be saved in a different process. On the Agent Server, persistence is handled for you. I would use LangSmith traces to see where each run stops. Finally, I would reproduce the bug with a script that triggers the interrupt, then resumes it, and check the result.
keyPoints: Studio works because langgraph dev manages the local run
Check that the thread_id is stable across the pause and resume
Make sure the client detects the interrupt and resumes with Command
Check for InMemorySaver across workers or restarts; use traces to locate the stop
